“Do not listen to the creature. If you come with us, I can protect you from what is awakening inside your blood.”

Neither of them offers you freedom without a price.

The village burns around you, and the silver echo beneath your skin continues to sound.

For once, the decision is yours.

choices.text: Gather the surviving villagers and lead them along the main road to Highspire Garrison.
Venture alone into the mist-covered crags to hunt the scattered Coven scouts.

text.content:
You raise your arm and point north towards the jagged peaks.

“Look at the horizon!” you roar over the crackle of the flames.

For a moment, neither man responds. Marek's attention remains fixed on Balor, while the Fae stands amid the shattered remains of his iron cage, silver rings glowing faintly at his wrists. Both are poised to continue their confrontation, each convinced that the other must be defeated before anything else can matter.

You refuse to let them ignore what is coming.

“Look!”

This time, your voice carries across the square with enough authority to turn the heads of the nearest Wardens. You point towards the mountains, where the last remnants of evening light should be catching the snow-streaked peaks.

Instead, the horizon is disappearing.

A bank of grey-black fog spills down the mountainside. It does not drift like ordinary mist, following the contours of the land or gathering in the hollows. It pours over the ridges in thick, deliberate waves, swallowing trees and boulders as though the mountains themselves are dissolving into shadow.

The wind changes.

It rushes through the village carrying the smell of ozone, wet stone, and charred bone. Your throat tightens. The taste of metal settles on your tongue, and the magic beneath your skin answers with a sudden, painful throb.

Somewhere within the fog, a horn sounds.

The note is deep enough to vibrate through the cobbles beneath your boots. It is followed by another, then a third. Each blast comes closer, rolling down the valley like thunder.

The villagers fall silent.

You recognise the fear spreading across their faces. They have already watched their homes burn. They have seen the dead and wounded carried through the streets, and they have witnessed a creature of legend break free from a cage of iron. They have nothing left to give a second army.

“The Bone Horde is moving,” you say, looking between Marek and Balor. “If we fight now, none of us survive sunrise.”

Marek turns towards the mountains.

The movement is small, controlled, but you notice how quickly his expression changes. His grey eyes narrow as he studies the advancing fog, searching for its edges, its speed, and the ground it covers. The dark coat around his shoulders stirs in the sudden chill wind. His fingers tighten around the iron-topped stave until the leather binding creaks.

For the first time since you met him, he appears to be calculating a problem he cannot solve simply by issuing an order.

“That is impossible,” one of the surviving Wardens mutters.

Marek silences him with a glance.

“Not impossible,” he says. “Unexpected.”

“Is that what you call it when an army comes to kill you?” Balor asks.

The Fae has lowered his arms. The silver light around his wrists has dimmed to a low simmer, though the broken rings still pulse against his skin. He watches the ridge with a stillness that seems almost unnatural. His earlier amusement has vanished, replaced by an expression you cannot quite interpret.

Recognition, perhaps.

Or dread.

“You know what that is,” you say.

Balor does not look at you. “I know what it means when the dead begin marching.”

Another horn sounds, closer than the last.

From somewhere beyond the fog comes the grinding crash of something enormous moving through the forest. Trees crack. A flock of black birds erupts from the ridge, wheeling away from the mountains in frantic confusion. Beneath the horns, you hear a faint, rhythmic clatter, like hundreds of bones knocking together.

The Bone Horde.

You have heard stories, of course. Everyone has. Old tales told beside winter hearths, when the darkness outside seemed to press its face against the windows. Armies assembled from the remains of ancient warriors. Skeletons clad in rusted armour, marching beneath banners woven from burial shrouds. Some said they were the remnants of a kingdom that had refused to die. Others claimed they were the servants of a god whose name had been struck from every surviving scripture.

You had always assumed the stories were meant to frighten children.

Now the mountains are vomiting ash, and something in the valley is answering the horns.

“How many?” Marek asks.

Balor finally turns his head.

“Enough.”

“That is not a number.”

“It is the only answer you need.”

Marek's jaw tightens. “If they reach the village before the garrison can reinforce the northern approach, the entire valley becomes indefensible.”

“Then stop wasting time trying to put chains around everything you fear,” you say.

The words escape before caution can restrain them.

Several Wardens turn towards you. One lifts his stave, but Marek raises a hand and stops him.

You continue before either man can interrupt.

“Your people are scattered. His magic is weakened. The village is burning, and the road is filling with smoke. You can keep fighting over who owns me, or you can work out how to get everyone out alive.”

Marek studies you with renewed attention.

You can almost see him revising his assessment. Until now, he has treated you as a problem to be contained, a bloodline to be studied, a key to some ancient mechanism he believes belongs to his order. You have no idea whether your words have changed his opinion of you, but they have forced him to acknowledge that you are more than an object standing between two opposing powers.

Balor's gaze settles on you as well.

There is a faint, dangerous curve to his mouth.

“Careful, little key,” he murmurs. “You are beginning to sound like someone who expects to be obeyed.”

“Would you prefer I let you two finish killing each other?”

“Not particularly.”

“Then be quiet.”

For the briefest instant, something resembling genuine amusement crosses his face.

Marek does not share it.

He turns to his remaining Wardens and begins issuing orders. Two are sent to retrieve the injured. Another is instructed to carry a message to the garrison, warning that the northern approach is threatened. The others are ordered to secure the road and prevent panic among the survivors.

His voice is calm again, but the speed of his instructions betrays the urgency beneath it.

You watch him carefully. He is not abandoning his objective. Men like Marek rarely abandon anything simply because circumstances become inconvenient. He is changing his strategy, buying time until he can return to the question of your bloodline.

Balor understands that too.

“Your truce will last until you believe you have the advantage,” he tells Marek.

“And yours will last until you find a way to escape.”

“Then perhaps we understand one another.”

The two men exchange a look that promises no friendship whatsoever.

Marek turns back to you.

“A temporary reprieve, mortal. We will negotiate proper terms at the perimeter.”

He signals his Wardens to fall back.

The order is obeyed reluctantly. Several of them keep their staves trained on Balor as they retreat, while others glance repeatedly towards the mountains. Their formation has lost its earlier precision. Fear is making them human again.

Balor remains where he is, watching the fog descend.

You notice that he has shifted slightly closer to you, though whether it is an attempt to protect you or simply to keep you within reach, you cannot tell.

“What is the Bone Horde?” you ask quietly.

“An army that should have remained buried.”

“That tells me nothing.”

“It tells you enough to understand why we cannot afford another battle here.”

You look towards the ridge. The fog has reached the lower slopes now, and beneath its dark canopy, pale shapes flicker between the trees. Too distant to identify. Too numerous to count.

“Can it be stopped?”

Balor's expression hardens.

“Everything can be stopped. The question is what it costs.”

Behind you, a woman calls for help. A wounded villager lies beneath a fallen beam, and two others struggle to lift the timber from his legs. The village militia is gathering near the road, looking to anyone who seems capable of telling them what to do.

Their eyes find you.

You could lead them towards Highspire Garrison, where walls and organised defences might give them a chance. Your willingness to stand between Marek and Balor has earned you something more valuable than either man's approval: the attention of people who have watched you refuse to abandon them.

Or you could offer yourself as a hostage in the Coven camp, forcing Marek to honour the truce while the survivors escape. It would place you directly in his hands, but it might prevent his Wardens from turning on Balor before the Bone Horde arrives.

Neither choice is safe.

The horns sound again, and this time the ground trembles beneath your feet.

You turn towards the gathering villagers.

Whatever happens next, someone must make a decision before the fog reaches the road.

choices.text: Lead the organized village militia to Highspire as a recognized field commander.
Offer yourself as a temporary hostage in the Coven camp to guarantee they don't break the truce.

text.content:
The air in the subterranean passage is bitterly cold, smelling of ancient wet slate, dry dust, and something faintly metallic that catches at the back of your throat. Above you, the heavy thud of garrison boots echoes through the ceiling. Soldiers patrol the corridors, moving between the barracks, armory, and battlements, completely unaware that someone has entered the oldest foundations of their keep.

Someone who, according to the Coven's own Scholar, might be the key to everything they have spent centuries trying to contain.

You press one hand against the damp wall and listen.

The footsteps pass overhead. A voice calls an order, followed by the scrape of a weapon against stone. Then the sounds fade, leaving only the distant groan of timber and the steady drip of water somewhere in the darkness.

You have not come here by accident.

Marek's revelations in the village square have changed the shape of everything you thought you understood. Your ancestors did not merely live in Highspire. They helped construct the wards beneath it, pouring their blood into the foundations to seal something dangerous below the earth. The Coven inherited the fortress, its records, and the authority to decide what those wards meant.

Your family inherited the consequences.

You descend another flight of narrow steps, following the fragments of memory that have begun surfacing since the village burned. You remember a phrase spoken by an older relative when you were young, a warning about old stones and doors that should never be opened. You had assumed it was one of those family sayings whose meaning had been lost over generations.

Now the words seem less like a warning and more like an instruction.

*The blood remembers where the stone forgets.*

The passage opens into a cavernous chamber.

You stop at its threshold.

A massive circular archway rises from the floor ahead, carved from dark basalt and framed by pillars that disappear into the shadows above. Its surface is covered in intricate runes, some worn almost smooth by time, others sharply defined as though they were carved yesterday. A faint, pulse-like light travels through them in slow waves.

You feel each pulse in your chest.

The rhythm matches your heartbeat.

You approach cautiously, watching the light travel around the arch. The sensation beneath your skin strengthens with every step, becoming a low pressure in your palms and a strange warmth behind your sternum. Whatever your ancestors did here, some part of it recognises you.

Beside the archway lies a shattered iron alcove. Its twisted frame rests against the wall, and its floor is littered with centuries-old warding components: broken silver pins, fragments of bone-white ceramic, corroded chains, and thin plates of metal engraved with symbols you cannot read.

A layer of dust covers everything except a narrow path leading towards the arch.

Someone has been here recently.

You crouch beside the debris, careful not to disturb the components. The iron is old, but the damage is not. Several pieces have been torn away from their original fittings, leaving fresh scratches in the stone. Whatever happened here, it was violent enough to damage a mechanism designed to survive centuries.

A metallic hum rises from deep within the chamber.

It is quiet at first, barely distinguishable from the vibration of the keep above. Then it deepens, passing through the soles of your boots and into your bones. The runes brighten.

Your hand moves towards the arch before you consciously decide to reach for it.

You stop yourself.

The last time your blood answered an ancient magic, Highspire burned.

You cannot afford to mistake recognition for safety.

Your attention settles on the shattered iron alcove. Even in the poor light, you recognise the logic of its construction. The casing was designed to protect a mechanical assembly, with interlocking plates and a counterweight system built into the surrounding stone.

The damage looks catastrophic, but the underlying structure remains intact.

You kneel and brush away the dust, tracing the grooves where the plates once fitted together. One narrow seam runs behind the iron casing, almost invisible beneath the corrosion. You press against it, and a small section shifts inward with a reluctant click.

A reset lever emerges from the darkness.

You recognise the arrangement immediately. The original mechanism would have required someone to release the pressure before the archway's inner wards could be disturbed. Anyone who attempted to force the lock without resetting the assembly would have triggered a trap beneath the floor.

You test the lever gently. It moves a fraction, then catches.

A second adjustment releases it.

The hum changes pitch.

You have found a way to bypass the pressure trap without dismantling the mechanism or risking a direct surge of magic. For the first time since entering the chamber, you feel the familiar satisfaction of solving a problem with your own hands.

The old builders were clever.

They simply did not expect you to be here.

You study the dark residue staining the archway.

At first, it resembles ordinary grime, a mixture of dust and mineral deposits accumulated over centuries. But the colour is wrong, too deep and glossy in the cracks between the stones. When you bring your hand close, the metallic smell strengthens.

You recognise the pattern from your work with blood and injury, though nothing living could have produced a stain like this.

It is coagulated blood-magic.

The residue has dried into the stone itself, forming a network of channels that follow the runes around the arch. Some channels remain dark and dormant. Others pulse faintly with the same rhythm as your heartbeat.

You understand, with the unnerving certainty that sometimes comes when your hands know what to do before your mind catches up, that the magic has been designed to respond to a living bloodline.

But it is also designed to punish the wrong touch.

A necrotic lashback would travel through the blood-magic and strike whoever disturbed the seal. You can see where previous attempts to activate the arch have left blackened marks on the stone.

You identify a narrow section where the residue thins, close to the base of the left pillar. The pattern resembles a wound that has been carefully closed, leaving one small point where pressure can be applied without tearing the surrounding tissue.

You place your palm against that point.

The stone is cold enough to hurt.

You breathe slowly and wait for the pulse beneath your skin to settle into the rhythm of the runes. When you feel the two patterns align, you press gently.

The metallic hum softens.

The dark residue brightens, not with flame but with a deep red glow, and the pressure behind your sternum eases. You have found the place where the blood-lock can recognise you without striking back.

The knowledge frightens you more than the danger.

Somewhere in your family history, someone knew exactly how this would work.

You circle the chamber's perimeter, allowing your eyes to adjust to the shadows before moving closer to the archway.

The floor is uneven, scattered with fragments of broken stone and rusted metal. At first glance, the path towards the centre appears clear. Then you notice the faintest glimmer crossing one of the flagstones.

A tripwire.

You crouch, studying the floor from a different angle. Hair-thin strands stretch between tiny holes drilled into the stone, almost invisible beneath the dust. They are arranged in overlapping patterns, creating a perimeter around the archway.

Your hunting instincts take over.

You have spent enough time in the forest to know that the most dangerous part of a trap is often the section that looks harmless. You follow the lines with your eyes, searching for the places where one wire crosses another and where a careless step would trigger the mechanism.

The trap is old, but age has not made it safe. Several wires remain taut, their surfaces coated with a faint black sheen. Others have snapped, leaving gaps that appear to offer a direct route across the chamber.

You do not trust them.

Instead, you move along the outer edge, testing each flagstone with the careful pressure of your boot before transferring your weight. Twice, you discover hidden channels beneath the dust. Once, you hear a soft click from somewhere under the floor and freeze until the sound dies away.

At last, you reach a raised section of stone beside the archway.

From here, you can see that the tripwires form a deliberate pattern around the entrance, designed to funnel intruders towards the central pressure plate. Whoever built the trap expected anyone approaching the vault to rush towards the obvious door.

You have survived by refusing to take the obvious path.

The archway's runes pulse as you draw near. Your blood answers, and for one unsettling instant you feel as though something on the other side has turned its attention towards you.

You stand before the circular archway.

The metallic hum deepens until it seems to fill the entire chamber. Fine dust trembles on the ledges above. The runes brighten in sequence, tracing a path around the basalt ring before converging on a small depression at its centre.

A place for a hand.

A place for blood.

You remember Marek's words in the village square: your ancestors poured their lifeblood into the bedrock beneath Highspire Garrison. You had thought he was describing a ritual performed long ago, an act whose consequences belonged to the dead.

But the archway is responding to you now.

You could channel the power through the old conduits, strengthening the keep's upper defences against whatever is approaching from the mountains. It might protect the soldiers and refugees gathered above, but it would also reveal how much control you have over the ancient wards.

Or you could leave the central mechanism untouched and search for another route into the keep. Somewhere above, Commander Vane holds authority over the garrison. His private quarters may contain maps, records, or evidence that the Coven has concealed the true purpose of the vault.

Either path will take you deeper into a conflict that began long before you were born.

You place your hand against the cold basalt and feel the pulse of your ancestors moving beneath it.

The vault waits.

choices.text: Manipulate the vault's ancient blood-lock to channel extra power directly into the keep's upper defenses.
Bypass the main vault core entirely and search for a secret stair leading up into Commander Vane's private quarters.

text.content:
The low hum of the bedrock grows stronger as you enter the central core.

The passage narrows before opening into a circular chamber buried deep beneath Highspire Garrison. The ceiling disappears into darkness, supported by enormous pillars of black basalt. Their surfaces are carved with overlapping runes, some so ancient that the edges have worn smooth, others glowing faintly with a violet light that pulses in time with your heartbeat.

The air is warmer here, though the stone beneath your fingers remains cold. It smells of greasy oil, damp slate, and the sharp metallic tang of magic held too long in one place.

Ancient brass conduits run along the walls like thick roots. Their surfaces are darkened by centuries of preserved oil, and their joints are reinforced with iron collars engraved with the same symbols that circle the vault entrance. Every few moments, a faint shudder travels through the pipes, accompanied by a deep mechanical groan.

You watch the movement travel from one conduit to another.

The system is still functioning.

Whatever your ancestors built beneath the fortress, the Coven has kept it alive.

You move towards the centre of the chamber, where several conduits converge around a raised platform. At its heart stands a column of dark stone encircled by a framework of brass rings. Narrow channels have been cut into the platform, carrying a faint silver light from the central column towards the surrounding walls.

The light disappears into the bedrock.

You realise that the conduits do not simply carry power through the fortress. They direct it, distributing the force of the ancient seal into the foundations above. The keep's walls, its gates, and perhaps even its defensive wards are connected to this chamber.

The fortress is not merely built over the vault.

It is part of the mechanism that holds it closed.

The thought settles heavily in your mind.

Marek had described your ancestors as ward-keepers, but he had spoken as though their work were an inconvenience inherited by the Coven. Standing here, surrounded by the machinery of their labour, you begin to understand how much of the fortress depends on the bloodline he intends to control.

You are not simply a key to a door.

You may be part of the lock itself.

Your attention turns towards the framework surrounding the central column. You recognise the logic of the assembly almost immediately. The brass rings are not decorative. Each connects to a counterweight hidden inside the surrounding pillars, allowing the system to redirect the pressure travelling through the conduits.

It is an ingenious design, though the passage of centuries has left several components badly worn.

You crouch beside the nearest housing and brush away a thick layer of dust. Beneath it, a small brass plate bears a sequence of engraved marks. You recognise them as maintenance indicators, similar in principle to the alignment marks used in older mechanical assemblies, though these have been arranged to account for the flow of magic rather than ordinary force.

One mark is out of alignment.

You follow the connected mechanism until you find a rusted release lever concealed behind a narrow iron panel. Its handle is almost seized in place, and the surrounding casing has been distorted by years of pressure.

You test it carefully.

The lever resists, then moves a fraction.

A deep click sounds from inside the pillar.

You stop and listen. The hum changes pitch, becoming lower and steadier. One of the brass rings rotates slowly around the central column, while a second slides into position beneath it.

You understand what has happened.

The lower cellars were once connected to the same network, probably to supply the vault's holding chambers with enough energy to maintain their restraints. Those sections have been abandoned, but their conduits remain active. By releasing the counterweight, you can divert that unused pressure towards the main keep gate.

You pull the lever into its new position.

The mechanism answers with a heavy metallic clank. Along the wall, a series of small indicators illuminate one after another, tracing the route of the redirected energy towards the fortress above.

You have strengthened the main gate without disturbing the central seal.

It is a small victory, but a meaningful one. You have proved that the machinery can be understood and manipulated without blindly unleashing whatever lies beneath it.

You rise, wiping the grime from your fingers.

For the first time since entering the vault, the ancient mechanism feels less like a mystery and more like a problem you might actually solve.

You approach the nearest conduit and hold your hand just above its surface.

The vibration is immediate.

It passes through the air into your palm, then climbs your arm in a series of slow, measured pulses. You feel it in your teeth, behind your eyes, and deep in your chest, where the strange rhythm of your blood answers the hum beneath the fortress.

You place your hand against the brass.

The metal is unexpectedly warm.

For a moment, nothing happens. Then the violet light inside the conduit brightens, illuminating the dark lines of your fingers against its surface. The pulse beneath your skin falls into step with the current.

You draw a sharp breath.

The connection is not a voice, exactly, nor a vision. It is an impression of movement and purpose: power flowing down one channel, dividing at a junction, and rising through another. You sense the immense weight of the keep above, the pressure of its walls and towers resting on the ancient foundations.

You also sense interruptions.

Several branches of the network are dimmer than the others. Some have been deliberately closed, while others flicker as though the mechanisms controlling them are failing. The largest interruption lies somewhere beyond the central column, where the current gathers before dividing towards the fortress.

You press your palm more firmly against the conduit.

The hum swells.

For one disorienting instant, you feel as though the entire structure is resting beneath your hand. The fortress above becomes a pattern of pressure and movement: soldiers crossing stone corridors, gates trembling in their frames, warding sigils glowing along the outer walls.

Farther away, beyond the foundations, you sense the dark weight of something sealed beneath the bedrock.

You recoil.

The light dims, and the connection breaks.

Your heart pounds against your ribs. The conduit returns to its former rhythm, but the knowledge remains. You have not commanded the mechanism, and you have not altered its flow. You have simply felt the system as it exists, learning where the power travels and where it falters.

Your bloodline recognises the ancient seal.

Whether the seal recognises you in return is a more troubling question.

You lower your hand and study the conduits with renewed caution. There is more to this chamber than a network of old pipes. It is a living arrangement of magic, stone, and inherited obligation, and you have only begun to understand how deeply your ancestors bound themselves to it.

A sudden metallic groan interrupts your thoughts.

The sound comes from the far side of the chamber, where a heavy stone slab has been fitted into the wall. Dust trickles from its upper edge. For several seconds, nothing moves. Then the slab shifts inward by a fraction, grinding against its stone frame.

You step back.

A narrow line of darkness appears along one side. The slab moves again, slowly withdrawing into the wall until a passage is revealed behind it.

Cold air spills into the chamber.

Unlike the dry, metallic smell of the core, this air carries the scent of wet earth and something faintly sweet, like old leaves left to decay beneath snow. The passage beyond slopes downwards before bending sharply out of sight.

You approach the opening but do not cross it immediately.

The wall beside the passage bears another set of markings. They are older than the inscriptions surrounding the central column, carved directly into the basalt rather than added as part of the mechanical framework. You recognise the recurring shape of the ancestral seal, though here it has been divided into three interlocking sections.

One section glows faintly beneath your gaze.

The others remain dark.

You cannot tell whether the passage has opened because you adjusted the mechanism, because your bloodline has awakened the vault, or because something deeper has noticed your presence.

A quiet click echoes from within the newly revealed corridor.

Then another.

The sound travels away from you, deeper beneath the fortress, as though a sequence of old locks is releasing one after another.

You glance back towards the central core. The conduits continue to hum, and the light along the brass framework remains steady. Whatever has changed, the mechanism has not collapsed. For now, the upper keep remains supported by the ancient system your ancestors left behind.

But the passage offers a route into the fortress's hidden architecture, beyond the chambers the Coven appears to use.

You have a choice: remain near the core and continue studying the machinery, or follow the newly opened junction into the older foundations. Somewhere ahead may lie the central junction chamber, where the conduits converge and the full design of the vault becomes clearer.

You take one final look at the runes.

The pulse beneath your skin answers them once.

Then you step into the passage.

choices.text: Follow the subterranean junction toward the central junction chamber.

text.content:
You squeeze through a hairline crack in the masonry, turning your shoulders sideways to force your way into the narrow space beyond.

The stone scrapes against your back. Dust catches in your throat, and for several uncomfortable seconds you are wedged between two sections of ancient wall, with barely enough room to draw a full breath. You feel along the darkness until your fingers find a narrow ledge. Using it for leverage, you pull yourself forward.

The passage opens suddenly.

You emerge onto a spiral staircase, its stone steps worn smooth by centuries of forgotten feet. The walls curve tightly around you, rising into darkness above. Narrow arrow loops have been cut into the outer masonry, allowing thin slivers of moonlight to filter down through the stairwell. Dust motes drift lazily through the pale beams, disturbed only by the movement of air from somewhere higher in the keep.

You pause to recover your breath.

Above you, the garrison is awake.

Muffled voices echo down the staircase, accompanied by the occasional scrape of boots against stone. You cannot make out every word, but certain phrases carry clearly enough.

"...fog reached the northern ridge..."

"...no word from the outer watch..."

"...Commander wants the gates reinforced before midnight."

The Bone Horde is drawing closer.

You look down at your hands. There is still dust beneath your fingernails from the subterranean passage, and a faint ache runs through your palms where the ancient magic answered your blood. You have escaped the vault core without activating its central mechanism, but you have not escaped the consequences of what you discovered.

The keep above you is full of people who believe they are defending a fortress.

Very few of them appear to understand what lies beneath it.

You begin to climb.

The staircase winds upwards through the foundations, passing sealed doorways and narrow maintenance chambers. Some have been bricked over so thoroughly that you can barely distinguish their outlines. Others bear the faded marks of the Coven, silver sigils stamped into the stone beside rusted iron hinges.

You notice that several of the older markings have been deliberately scratched away.

Someone has tried to erase the history of this place.

At the next landing, you hear a pair of guards approaching from above. Their conversation grows louder as they descend the corridor beyond the staircase.

"...Vane says nobody leaves the walls without permission."

"Then I hope he has a better plan than standing on the battlements waiting to be buried."

"Keep your voice down. The Scholar's people are everywhere."

You flatten yourself against the wall.

The footsteps pass the entrance to the stairwell. One guard pauses, and you hear the faint jingle of keys. For a moment, you are certain he has noticed something. Then his companion calls from farther down the corridor, and the man moves on.

You wait until the echoes disappear.

The staircase feels different now. It is no longer simply a hidden route into the keep. It is a narrow boundary between two worlds: the ancient machinery below and the desperate military order above.

You have entered a place where both are beginning to fail.

You move with silent, measured steps, placing your feet carefully along the outer edges of the stairs. Years of tracking through woodland have taught you to notice the small things that betray movement: loose stones, brittle twigs, patches of damp ground that hold a footprint.

Here, the dangers are different, but the principles remain the same.

A thin layer of dry mortar debris covers several steps. You recognise the pattern of disturbance where previous footsteps have shifted the dust, revealing the safest route upwards. You avoid the loose fragments and step over a narrow crack in the stone before it can catch beneath your boot.

At another landing, you stop when a faint vibration travels through the wall.

Someone is moving along the corridor above, their weight shifting from one foot to the other. You wait until the sound moves away before continuing.

Your progress is slow, but almost completely silent.

By the time you reach the upper staircase, you have learned to distinguish the ordinary noises of the keep from the movements of its patrols. You know when a guard is approaching, when someone has stopped to speak, and when a corridor has been left temporarily unattended.

The skills that once kept you alive in the forest are proving just as useful among stone walls and armed soldiers.

You pause at every landing, listening closely before continuing.

The keep has its own rhythm. Boots move along the upper corridors at regular intervals, while voices gather and disperse around the main stairwells. Every so often, a door opens and closes, followed by the clatter of equipment being moved.

You begin to map the patrols in your head.

Two guards appear to be assigned to the northern corridor, passing the staircase at intervals. Another patrol moves between the armory and the battlements. Somewhere above, a group of soldiers is receiving orders, their voices overlapping whenever the corridor doors open.

You learn to distinguish the sound of a single guard from a larger patrol. You also discover that the old staircase does not carry sound evenly. Certain sections of the wall amplify voices, while others swallow them almost completely.

At one landing, you hear someone approaching and retreat into a narrow recess. The footsteps pass so close that you can hear the leather creak of the guard's boots.

You remain still until the sound fades.

By the time you reach the upper level, you have a rough understanding of the patrol routes and the moments when the corridors are least likely to be watched.

You are not invisible.

But you are beginning to understand where the keep fails to look.

The staircase ends at a narrow wooden door.

You press your ear against it.

Beyond lies a corridor filled with the familiar sounds of military activity. Someone is speaking in a low, urgent voice. A chair scrapes across stone. Then comes the unmistakable clink of metal as a weapon is placed against a wall.

You test the handle.

Locked.

For a moment, you consider forcing it, but the door is old and the hinges are likely to complain loudly. Instead, you examine the surrounding masonry. A narrow gap runs along the frame, and beneath it you can see a faint line of light.

There is another way out.

You follow the wall to the left, where the staircase narrows into a shallow recess. A section of stonework has been fitted with a concealed catch, almost indistinguishable from the surrounding masonry. You press against it.

Nothing happens.

You try again, this time pushing slightly upwards.

A soft click sounds.

The wooden door shifts outwards by a fraction, revealing a narrow space behind it. You ease it open just enough to slip through, then close it carefully behind you.

You find yourself in a concealed alcove behind a tapestry in the upper keep hallway.

The tapestry depicts an ancient battle: armoured figures standing beneath a pale sun, their weapons raised against a procession of shadowed creatures. The stitching is faded, and several sections have been repaired with newer thread. You recognise the heraldic symbol at its centre as the mark of Highspire's ruling garrison.

The irony is not lost on you.

The keep's official history hangs on the wall above a hidden passage built by people whose names have been forgotten.

You lift one corner of the tapestry and look out.

The corridor is wider than the staircase, lined with iron sconces and narrow windows overlooking the inner courtyard. Soldiers move between the doors, carrying bundles of arrows, rolled maps, and crates of supplies. A pair of officers stand beside a table covered in parchment, arguing over the placement of defensive positions.

Beyond them, you can see a staircase leading towards the central keep.

A distant horn sounds from outside.

The officers fall silent.

"Another signal from the northern watch," one says.

"How close?"

"Closer than the last."

The second officer rubs his forehead. "Then we need Vane's orders before the next shift."

They gather their papers and hurry down the corridor.

You remain behind the tapestry, watching until the last soldier disappears.

There is a strange sensation beneath your skin. It is faint, but unmistakable: the same pulse you felt in the vault below. Somewhere beyond the corridor, the ancient conduits continue to carry their hidden current through the fortress.

The keep is built upon a secret that the people living inside it do not understand.

And now you know how to reach it.

You could turn back towards the hidden staircase, but that would mean abandoning the opportunity to discover what the garrison knows. Commander Vane's private quarters may contain maps of the foundations, records of the old ward-keepers, or orders concerning the approaching Bone Horde.

You have no guarantee that the information will be useful.

You have even less certainty that Vane will welcome an uninvited visitor.

But you have reached the upper keep without being discovered. For the moment, that advantage is yours.

You draw the tapestry back into place and step into the corridor.

The central junction lies ahead.

choices.text: Step out into the shadowed corridor toward the central junction.

text.content:
The passage narrows before opening without warning.

You step through the final archway and find yourself standing above a cavernous vault, its ceiling lost in darkness. The chamber lies directly beneath the heart of Highspire Garrison, far below the barracks, the commander's quarters and the great stone gatehouse. Its walls are carved from black basalt, their surfaces covered in lines of ancient script that catch the faintest suggestion of violet light.

Water drips steadily from somewhere overhead.

Each drop strikes a dark pool in the centre of the flagstones, sending small ripples across its otherwise motionless surface. The sound is strangely loud in the enormous chamber. You hear it echo against the stone, returning a fraction of a second later, as though the vault itself is listening.

You approach the pool.

There are no reflections in it. Not of the ceiling, nor the pale light behind you, nor your own face. Only darkness.

A narrow walkway crosses the chamber towards a raised platform. At its centre stands a column of obsidian, bound with bands of tarnished silver. The same ancestral markings you encountered in the tunnels have been carved into its surface. They form a series of interlocking circles, each one connected to the next by fine grooves.

You recognise the pattern.

Not entirely. The knowledge is older than anything you were taught, buried beneath generations of forgotten history. Yet something in your blood responds to it. The column is not simply decorative. It is part of the foundation anchor, the mechanism that binds the ancient vault beneath Highspire to the bedrock surrounding it.

The fortress has been built around this place.

For three hundred years, perhaps longer, its walls have drawn strength from the same magic that keeps whatever lies beneath the valley imprisoned.

A faint vibration passes through the floor.

You look down.

The water in the pool has begun to tremble.

Then the entire chamber shudders.

The sound comes from deep below, a tremendous grinding groan that travels through the foundations and into your bones. Dust falls from the ceiling. One of the silver bands around the central column gives a sharp metallic crack.

You stumble against the walkway railing.

For a moment, the violet markings flare brightly enough to illuminate the entire vault. You see the lines running beneath the flagstones, branching into the walls and disappearing downwards through the bedrock.

Something is disturbing the network.

Then you hear it.

A scrape. A pause. Another scrape.

Metal against stone.

The sound rises from the deepest catacombs beneath you. It is accompanied by the muffled rhythm of heavy tools striking rock.

Obsidian picks.

The Coven's ward-breakers.

They are attempting to breach the foundation anchor from below.

Your stomach tightens. The vault's ancient defences were designed to withstand pressure from the outside, but the anchor itself is vulnerable. If the ward-breakers reach the central binding, they could sever the fortress from its foundations. The resulting collapse might destroy the garrison, but the consequences could be far worse. The old seal beneath Highspire would be left exposed.

You move towards the central column, placing one hand against its cold surface.

A pulse answers your touch.

It travels up your arm, through your shoulder and into your chest. For a heartbeat, you feel the entire fortress as though it were an extension of your own body. The outer walls. The gatehouse. The watchtowers. The tunnels beneath the barracks.

You sense the strain running through the ancient network.

The foundation anchor is weakening.

And then another sound reaches you.

Shouting.

It comes from somewhere above, distorted by the ventilation shaft that descends through the upper levels of the keep. You hear the clash of steel, the sharp command of an officer and the unmistakable crash of something heavy striking a rooftop.

You turn towards the shaft.

The voices are close enough now to distinguish.

“Get the gatehouse roof secured!”

“Where is Commander Vane?”

A second impact shakes dust from the shaft's stone lining.

The Coven has launched an attack from above as well.

Infiltrators have reached the roof of the main gatehouse. They are targeting the command position, and if they reach Commander Vane, the garrison could lose its leadership before anyone understands what is happening beneath their feet.

You look between the dark stairwell descending into the lower catacombs and the narrow spiral staircase climbing towards the upper keep.

Two threats. Two places where your presence could make a difference.

You have seconds to decide.

A sudden flash of memory passes through you: the village green at dusk, the familiar warmth of Highspire's hearths, the ordinary lives that existed before the sky turned violet. The people sheltering behind these walls have already lost their homes. If the garrison falls, there may be nowhere left for them to go.

You cannot be everywhere.

But perhaps you can prevent one disaster before it becomes two.

The water in the central pool begins to move again. This time, the ripples travel against the direction of the falling droplets, spreading outwards from the centre as though something beneath the surface has drawn breath.

You step back.

Whatever the Coven is attempting, it is connected to the same ancient power that answers your blood. The foundation anchor may recognise you. It may even obey you. But you do not know what it will demand in return.

Above, another cry rings out.

“Commander! They're on the roof!”

Below, the scraping becomes louder.

You grip the stone railing, forcing yourself to think clearly. The ward-breakers are working towards a specific objective. They must believe that destroying the anchor will give the Coven control over the vault. If you stop them, you might preserve the garrison's defences and prevent the deeper seal from being disturbed.

But if Vane is killed, the soldiers may fracture into competing commands. The refugees could be left undefended, and the Coven would have a clear path into the keep.

The decision is not between safety and danger.

It is between two kinds of danger, each with consequences you may not be able to repair.

You glance once more at the central column.

The silver bands pulse faintly beneath your palm, responding to the blood in your veins. Somewhere far below, something strikes the bedrock again.

The whole fortress groans.

You turn towards the staircases.

There is no time to hesitate.

choices.text: Descend into the lowest catacombs to stop the ward-breakers at the foundation anchor.
Sprint up the spiral stair to defend Commander Vane on the gatehouse roof.

text.content:
Cold drizzle falls continuously over the lower bailey of Highspire Garrison.

The courtyard has become a sea of mud, makeshift canvas tents and exhausted families. Rainwater runs in narrow channels between the flagstones, carrying scraps of straw and ash towards the drains. Tents have been erected wherever there is space: beneath the covered walkways, against the stable walls and in the shadow of the inner gatehouse. Some are little more than blankets stretched over wooden poles.

Smoke rises lazily from a single central soup kettle. A long queue of hollow-eyed refugees winds around it, each person holding a bowl or whatever vessel they managed to bring from home. The smell of thin vegetable broth barely disguises the damp wool, unwashed bodies and smoke clinging to everyone's clothes.

You step through the crowded paths, your boots caked in thick clay.

Soldiers in grey cloaks stand atop the inner walls, keeping a strict eye on the crowd below. Their faces are difficult to read beneath their hoods. Some watch the refugees with sympathy; others regard them as a potential threat. You notice several have their hands resting near their sword hilts whenever anyone approaches the gatehouse.

A quartermaster pushes past a group of frightened children.

"Make way! Clear the cart line!"

The children scatter. One little boy slips in the mud, dropping a wooden toy that disappears beneath someone's boot. His mother pulls him upright and hurriedly draws him against her skirts.

The quartermaster does not stop.

"Supplies through here! If you want your rations, keep out of the way!"

You watch the cart he is directing. It carries sacks of grain, bundles of firewood and several wooden crates marked with the garrison's seal. The supplies are being taken towards the inner buildings, away from the people who need them most.

A woman near the soup kettle coughs violently into her sleeve. Her daughter, perhaps six years old, holds a bowl with both hands, shivering beneath a coat too large for her.

The garrison is feeding the refugees, but only just.

You had imagined Highspire as a place of refuge when you first saw its walls rising above the road. Standing here, you begin to understand that stone fortifications and soldiers do not necessarily make a place safe. There are too many people, too few supplies and too many frightened men attempting to impose order on a situation they cannot fully control.

A familiar voice calls through the mist.

"Elara?"

You turn.

Several villagers from Highspire have recognised you. Mara stands beside one of the tents, her shawl drawn tightly around her shoulders. Her face is pale with exhaustion, but relief crosses it when she sees you.

"Thank goodness. We wondered if you had made it here."

Elsie is beside her, wrapped in a blanket. She looks better than she did during the fever, although her cheeks are still hollow and her eyes follow every movement around the courtyard.

Tomas emerges from behind a cart, carrying a bundle of firewood beneath one arm.

"Thought you'd be somewhere near the trouble," he says. "You always did have a talent for finding it."

His attempt at humour is unconvincing, but there is genuine relief in his expression.

Other villagers gather as word spreads. Some ask whether their homes can ever be recovered. Others want to know whether the strange fires have stopped, whether the soldiers can protect them and whether anyone has seen their missing relatives.

You have no answers for most of them.

Yet you notice something as they gather around you. They are waiting for you to speak. Not because you hold any official authority, but because they remember you from before the destruction. They remember the person who helped with injuries, repaired broken things, found lost children or simply listened when someone needed it.

For a moment, the courtyard feels less like a collection of frightened strangers.

You slip through the crowd unnoticed.

There is something useful about being overlooked. People speak more freely when they believe nobody important is listening. You hear arguments over ration portions, complaints about missing blankets and whispered accusations that the quartermaster is keeping supplies for the soldiers.

Near the stable entrance, two guards discuss the condition of the western wall.

"The mortar's splitting," one mutters. "Another strike like last night and the whole section will come down."

"Then pray they don't bring the siege engine forward."

You continue walking, taking in the details. The garrison has food, but not enough to sustain the refugees for long. Its soldiers are tired, its walls are damaged and its command structure appears increasingly concerned with controlling the population rather than preparing for what is coming.

You also notice that several supply carts have been redirected towards the inner buildings. The lower armory lies beyond them, guarded by only two soldiers.

It is information worth remembering.

A sudden commotion erupts near the inner gatehouse.

A guard captain stands in front of a family attempting to enter through the narrow passage. The father holds a small bundle of belongings, while his wife supports an elderly man whose legs appear unable to bear his weight. The elder's head hangs against her shoulder. His breathing is shallow and uneven.

"He's ill," the father insists. "He needs a bed. Somewhere dry. He's been getting worse since we left the village."

The captain raises one hand.

"And I have already told you that the infirmary is full. You cannot simply bring everyone through the gate."

"He's not everyone," the woman says. "Her voice breaks. "He's my father."

"Then find somewhere outside the walls until we have space."

The father steps forward, anger finally overcoming his fear.

"Outside? In this weather? He's barely conscious!"

Two soldiers move towards him.

The surrounding refugees begin to watch. A few mutter in agreement, but nobody steps forward. They have seen enough arguments with armed men to understand how quickly one can end.

The captain gestures towards the outer courtyard.

"Take him back. If he collapses, the infirmary will deal with him when they have time."

The woman clutches the old man's arm.

You look at the family, then at the soldiers. The elder needs warmth and medical attention. Even if the infirmary is full, there must be somewhere to shelter him. A storage room, a dry corner of the barracks, perhaps a place near the soup kettle where someone can monitor his breathing.

You also recognise the larger problem.

This is not simply one family being turned away. The garrison is beginning to treat the refugees as an inconvenience rather than the people it has sworn to protect. If that attitude spreads, the courtyard will become a place of resentment and desperation.

You could intervene. Whether the guards listen will depend partly on how much influence you have earned among the villagers.

Alternatively, the commotion provides an opportunity to move through the courtyard unnoticed. The lower supply armory is close by, and the militia will be of little use if there are no weapons left to equip them.

You glance towards the gatehouse.

The captain is waiting for the family to obey.

The decision is yours.

choices.text: Intervene with the guards using your standing to secure shelter and medicine for the refugees.
Slip into the lower supply armory to scout what weapons remain for the militia.

text.content:
High up on the icy crags of Frost-Spire Ridge, the wind howls through the pine needles.

You lie low behind a frost-covered boulder, its rough surface biting into your palms through your gloves. Below you, the valley road snakes through the fog, a pale ribbon of churned earth between steep slopes and dark woodland. The distant peaks disappear beneath a ceiling of low grey cloud.

You have been following the road since first light.

The journey has been difficult. Loose shale shifts beneath your boots, and several narrow ledges offer little protection from the sheer drops beside them. Twice, you have been forced to abandon the ridge and climb through dense pine forest to avoid being seen. Your clothes are damp, your fingers stiff with cold, and the food you carried has long since been eaten.

But the climb has brought you here.

Along the road below marches a vanguard column of Bone Coven scouts.

You draw your weapon and watch them through the mist.

Their formation is disciplined, though not particularly large. Three heavy ward-breakers occupy the centre of the column, each carrying an iron-bound ram or a long-handled tool designed to break magical defences. Their armour is dark, reinforced with strips of cold iron that catch the weak daylight. Behind them walks a small squad of initiates bearing obsidian torches.

The flames burn violet.

Even from this distance, you can feel the faint pressure of their magic. It prickles against your skin, an unpleasant sensation like standing too close to a thunderstorm.

There are perhaps twenty soldiers in total. A few scouts move ahead of the main group, searching the slopes and examining the road. Their movements are careful, their heads turning regularly towards the trees.

They are not travelling blindly.

They know the terrain may be dangerous.

You study their spacing, the weight of their equipment and the narrow section of road ahead. The gorge below you provides an obvious opportunity. Its walls rise steeply on either side, leaving little room for a large formation to manoeuvre. A fallen tree or a sudden rockslide could block the road entirely.

If you strike at the right moment, the vanguard could be trapped.

You might even destroy its leading ranks before the main army realises what has happened.

Your shortbow is already nocked.

You know the exact wind resistance down the gully. The gusts are strongest near the exposed western face, but the air settles briefly beneath the overhanging ridge. You have watched the scouts long enough to recognise the rhythm of their patrol. The lead soldier pauses every few moments to inspect the ground, while the one behind him keeps glancing towards the tree line.

You could take the lead scout before he even enters the pass.

The thought comes naturally. You have hunted through worse conditions than these, tracked wounded animals across frozen ground and waited motionless for hours to make a single clean shot.

The Coven soldiers are better armed than the creatures you once followed through the forest, but they are still vulnerable. Their armour cannot protect every joint, and their obsidian torches may be powerful, but they are not weapons designed for an enemy they cannot see.

For the first time since leaving Highspire, you feel entirely certain of your abilities.

You hold a heavy rock in your hand, examining the loose shale scattered across the slope.

You have never considered yourself a soldier, but the mountains do not require military training. They require patience, observation and an understanding of how weight moves across unstable ground.

The slope above the gorge is steep. Several large shelves of shale sit precariously beneath a shelf of exposed stone. If you could dislodge them, the resulting avalanche would sweep across the road and bury anything caught beneath it.

You test the ground with your boot.

A few fragments tumble away, bouncing down the hillside before disappearing into the mist.

The sound makes you freeze.

One of the scouts looks up.

You lower yourself behind the boulder and remain still until he turns away. Your heart beats painfully against your ribs.

You are not certain how much force the slope would require, or whether the rockfall would behave as you expect. But you understand enough to know that the gorge is a natural trap. With the right timing, you could turn the mountain itself against the Coven.

The column continues towards the pass.

One of the ward-breakers stops beside a roadside marker. He removes a small object from his belt and presses it against the stone. A thin violet line spreads across the marker's surface.

You recognise the action as a form of magical surveying.

They are measuring the strength of the old boundaries.

A second ward-breaker approaches and points towards the mountains beyond the valley.

"That is the route," he says. "The upper road leads directly to the garrison's northern approach."

The other man shakes his head.

"Not until the anchor is weakened. The gatehouse will hold if we attack it too early."

You lean closer.

The foundation anchor.

The words confirm what you have begun to suspect. The Coven is not simply marching towards Highspire to destroy its walls. They intend to undermine the ancient magic beneath the fortress, perhaps opening something that has remained sealed for generations.

The initiates raise their torches. Their violet flames briefly burn brighter, illuminating a series of markings on the road. The soldiers move forward again, leaving the roadside marker glowing faintly behind them.

You look towards the gorge.

There are two choices.

You could attack now, using the narrow terrain to inflict serious damage before the vanguard reaches the main army. It would be dangerous, perhaps suicidal, but every hour gained might give Highspire more time to prepare.

Or you could remain unseen.

The column will eventually reveal its destination, its numbers and the direction of the main siege force. If you follow them carefully, you may discover where the ward-breakers intend to strike, how the Coven plans to breach the garrison and whether another force is approaching from the mountains.

Information could save more lives than a handful of dead soldiers.

But it would mean allowing them to continue towards the valley.

A gust of wind tears across the ridge, scattering loose snow from the branches. The cold reaches beneath your collar. You shift your weight, feeling the rock beneath your knee.

Below, the lead scout raises his hand.

The entire column stops.

He turns towards the ridge.

For one long moment, you are certain he has seen you.

Then he looks away and signals the others to continue.

You have little time before they enter the gorge.

If you strike now, you can slow their main war-host down by hours. But you will draw the entire vanguard's wrath straight up the ridge. If you follow them, you may learn something far more valuable, but you will have to watch them advance without interference.

You draw a slow breath.

The valley lies beneath you, hidden by fog. Somewhere beyond it are the people you left behind, and the fortress they now depend upon.

You settle your weapon into position.

The next move is yours.

choices.text: Set a lethal ambush in the narrow gorge to decimate the vanguard's lead ranks.
Shadow the column quietly from the ridgeline to map out their main siege strategy.

text.content:
The war room atop the Keep tower is thick with candle smoke and the scent of tallow.

A massive wooden map of the valley covers the central table, its carved hills and riverbeds marked with thin lines of charcoal. Heavy lead markers represent the garrison regiments, while smaller pieces of black iron indicate the known positions of the Bone Coven's forces. Someone has placed a dagger across the northern road, its blade pointing towards Highspire.

The room is crowded with officers. Their cloaks hang damp from the rain, and several have removed their helmets and laid them beside the map. The air is warm, but nobody seems comfortable. Every few moments, the distant rumble of thunder rolls across the valley, though the sky outside remains a dull, unbroken grey.

Commander Vane stands at the head of the table, flanked by three senior captains.

They are arguing.

"We cannot hold the outer walls with the numbers we have," says a broad-shouldered captain, striking the map with one finger. "The western watchtower is already damaged. If the Coven brings those iron rams against the northern gate, we'll lose the whole section."

"And if we abandon the outer walls," another captain replies, "we surrender the lower bailey. There are hundreds of refugees in those tents. We cannot simply retreat and leave them exposed."

"The lower gates are a liability," the third insists. "Collapse them before the enemy reaches them. We can hold the inner wall and force the Coven into the killing ground."

The first captain gives a bitter laugh.

"With what men? Half the militia have never held a weapon, and the other half are exhausted."

You enter.

The room falls silent.

Vane looks up. His weather-beaten face is grim, but there is something in his expression that resembles respect. He gestures for you to approach the table.

"You held the square, gave our people time to retreat, and foresaw the ash-fog," he says. "The captains are divided on whether to hold the outer walls or collapse the lower gates entirely. We need your call."

You glance down at the map.

The valley is represented in careful detail. The river bends around the eastern edge of the fortress, while the northern road climbs through a narrow pass before reaching the outer gate. Beyond it, the mountains rise in jagged layers. Small markers show the positions of the garrison's scouts, though several have been moved since the last report.

A red thread runs from the northern road towards the main gatehouse.

Another marks the lower approach, where the ground slopes towards the bailey.

You notice that the two routes converge near the outer wall. Any force approaching from the north will have to pass through the narrow valley before it can spread out around the fortress. That gives the garrison a natural advantage, provided it can prevent the enemy from reaching the walls intact.

The captains murmur nervously at your posture. You stand with your shoulders squared, meeting their scrutiny without lowering your eyes.

One of them begins to speak, apparently ready to question why someone with no military rank has been invited into the war room.

Vane silences him with a look.

"She was standing in the village square when the rest of us were still arguing about what the smoke meant," he says. "She recognised the threat before our scouts returned. If you have a better reason to dismiss her, Captain, I suggest you give it."

The captain closes his mouth.

You have no formal commission, but nobody in the room can deny what you did at Highspire. For now, that is enough.

You approach the table without rushing.

The captains continue watching you, but your measured manner seems to steady the atmosphere. You study the map before speaking, allowing the argument to settle rather than adding another voice to it.

Vane notices.

"Good," he says quietly. "Someone in this room is still thinking."

One of the captains shifts aside to give you room at the table. The movement is small, but it is an acknowledgement that your opinion will be heard.

You examine the markers again.

The garrison has three main advantages: the height of the walls, the narrow northern approach and the old fortifications built into the mountain. Its weaknesses are equally obvious. The outer battlements are damaged, the lower gates are exposed and the militia are poorly trained.

The Coven has cold iron, obsidian magic and soldiers who appear to understand the fortress's ancient defences better than the people currently occupying it.

You wonder how much of the garrison's strength depends on the hidden vault beneath the Keep. If the foundation anchor is compromised, the walls may not hold regardless of how many soldiers are stationed upon them.

"How long until the main force arrives?" you ask.

Vane looks towards the nearest captain.

"Scouts estimate before nightfall. The vanguard has already reached the northern pass. We have reports of ward-breakers carrying heavy equipment, and something larger moving behind them."

"An army?"

"Possibly. Or a siege engine."

The room falls quiet again.

You look at the northern road. The lead markers representing the garrison's strongest troops are clustered around the gatehouse. There are also two ballista positions on the main battlements, though the captains have apparently been arguing about whether to move them.

"Those weapons," you say, indicating the markers. "Are they operational?"

The broad-shouldered captain answers.

"Two are. One has a damaged turning mechanism. We have cold-iron bolts, but not enough to waste them."

"And the lower gates?"

"Reinforcement beams are available, but they would take several hours to install. If we collapse the gates instead, we would need to clear the passage first."

Vane folds his arms.

"Which is why we are having this conversation."

You look around the table.

Every decision will cost something. An aggressive defence could inflict serious damage on the Coven before they reach the walls, but it would expose the soldiers on the battlements to concentrated attack. A defensive withdrawal would protect the garrison's central position, but it would surrender ground and potentially trap refugees between the enemy and the inner wall.

You could also argue for a compromise, but the captains have already spent too long debating. Vane wants a clear decision, and the enemy is approaching.

A faint vibration travels through the floor.

The candles tremble.

One of the lead markers shifts slightly across the map.

Nobody speaks.

Vane looks towards the ceiling, then back at you.

"That is the third tremor in an hour," he says. "The engineers believe something is disturbing the foundations."

You remember the ancient markings beneath the fortress. The column of obsidian, the silver bands and the network of magic running through the bedrock. If the Coven is attempting to break the anchor, the battle may be decided beneath the walls rather than upon them.

But the immediate threat remains.

Vane places both hands on the table.

"Give me your recommendation, Elara. We will make the preparations now."

The captains wait.

You take one final look at the map, weighing the narrow northern approach against the vulnerable lower gates.

choices.text: Advise an aggressive forward defense on the main battlements using cold-iron ballistas.
Order the lower gates reinforced and prepare an elastic defense inside the inner bailey.

text.content:
The smell of burning bone and bitter elder-bark fills the air inside the Coven's forward war-camp.

Tall wooden pikes surround the perimeter, their black iron runes glowing with violet energy. The magic crackles whenever the freezing valley wind presses against the boundary, creating a faint barrier that keeps the worst of the weather at bay. Beyond it, the camp stretches across the muddy ground in ordered rows of dark canvas tents, supply wagons and guarded enclosures.

You can hear the sounds of an army preparing for war: the hammering of armourers, the rhythmic sharpening of blades and the low murmur of soldiers exchanging orders. Occasionally, a distant horn sounds from somewhere beyond the camp, followed by the answering calls of sentries.

This is not a temporary gathering of frightened soldiers.

The Coven has established a proper military position here. Its supplies are organised, its defences maintained and its commanders apparently confident that Highspire will eventually fall.

You are brought towards the largest tent at the centre of the encampment.

It is distinguished by the ancient bloodline seals painted across its dark canvas. The symbols are unfamiliar, although something about their arrangement makes your skin prickle. They resemble the markings you encountered beneath Highspire, particularly the interlocking circles surrounding the foundation anchor.

Whatever Marek is studying, it is connected to the same history buried beneath the fortress.

You were dragged into the war-camp in heavy iron chains after throwing yourself in front of Marek's blade at the gorge.

The journey has left your wrists raw and your shoulders aching. Every movement reminds you of the cold iron restraints, whose unpleasant chill seems to penetrate beyond your skin. The soldiers accompanying you have said very little. They have not needed to. Their weapons and the chains have made your position perfectly clear.

Yet your thoughts keep returning to the moment on the bridge.

You remember Balor's hand guiding yours through the leyline magic. The strange warmth of the connection, the silver light moving between your palms and the feeling that, for one brief moment, you had understood something ancient and enormous.

You remember the blade.

You remember choosing to step between it and him.

Whether Balor escaped or was captured remains uncertain. You have heard no confirmation, and the soldiers have refused to answer your questions.

The memory lingers like a stubborn ember against your skin.

Marek steps out of his bloodline-sealed tent into the firelight. His ivory mask gleams beneath the violet glow of the perimeter wards. He sets his binding staff aside and examines you with cold, clinical curiosity.

“You threw yourself in front of a Fae predator,” Marek says, his voice carrying a dark resonance. “You sacrificed your freedom for a creature that views your bloodline as nothing more than a key. Did you truly think he would turn back for you?”

You say nothing immediately.

Marek studies your face as though searching for evidence of regret.

You hold his gaze without flinching.

Marek notices the quiet confidence in your expression. His attention shifts briefly towards your bound wrists, then back to your eyes. Something in his manner changes. He had expected a frightened hostage, perhaps someone who would readily trade information for comfort or protection.

Instead, he seems to recognise that the wild magic has already taken root in your blood.

“You have been exposed to more of his power than I anticipated,” he observes. “That complicates matters.”

You do not tell him how much.

The Fae connection remains somewhere beneath your skin, faint but unmistakable. Even here, surrounded by cold iron and Coven wards, you can feel the possibility of that other magic waiting to answer you.

You hold his gaze without flinching.

Marek notices the quiet confidence in your expression. His attention shifts briefly towards your bound wrists, then back to your eyes. Something in his manner changes. He had expected a frightened hostage, perhaps someone who would readily trade information for comfort or protection.

Instead, he seems to recognise that the wild magic has already taken root in your blood.

“You have been exposed to more of his power than I anticipated,” he observes. “That complicates matters.”

You do not tell him how much.

The Fae connection remains somewhere beneath your skin, faint but unmistakable. Even here, surrounded by cold iron and Coven wards, you can feel the possibility of that other magic waiting to answer you.

Marek gestures towards the tent.

“Come. There are matters concerning your ancestry that we should discuss.”

The guards hesitate before releasing enough chain for you to walk. You are not freed, but the restraints are loosened sufficiently to allow you to enter.

Inside, the tent is warmer than the surrounding camp. A brazier burns beneath a suspended iron frame, and shelves along the canvas walls hold scrolls, sealed jars and carefully labelled fragments of bone. A large writing desk dominates the centre of the space. Its surface is covered with parchment, ink pots and several heavy books.

One volume lies open beneath a brass weight.

You recognise the markings.

They are almost identical to those carved into the foundation anchor beneath Highspire.

Marek notices your attention.

“Your ancestors understood something that the modern Coven has spent generations attempting to recover,” he says. “They understood how to bind living blood to the old structures of the world.”

He turns a page.

“Your bloodline was not simply involved in the creation of the vault. It was part of the mechanism that keeps it closed.”

You look at the symbols again.

“What exactly do you intend to do with me?”

Marek does not answer immediately. He removes one of his silver rings and places it beside the book.

“That depends on what you are willing to understand.”

You walk between the bone-adorned tents, flanked by two armed initiates.

Though you entered as a voluntary hostage to secure the temporary truce, your wrists are bound with heavy hemp cord soaked in cold-iron oil. The restraints are not particularly painful, but they make their purpose clear. The Coven may have agreed to negotiate, yet it has no intention of allowing you to wander freely through its military encampment.

You pass several soldiers gathered around a low fire. One looks up as you approach, his gaze lingering on your hands. Another mutters something to his companion, who glances towards the central tent.

You wonder what they have been told about you.

Perhaps that you are a dangerous bloodline relic. Perhaps that you are a bargaining tool. Or perhaps they have simply been instructed not to underestimate anyone who can make ancient wards respond to a touch.

In the centre of the camp stands Marek's tent, its dark canvas painted with ancient bloodline seals.

Marek steps out into the firelight, his ivory mask gleaming in the darkness.

“You have remarkable nerve for a mortal,” he says, his voice echoing with dark resonance. “You sit in our camp while your people cower behind Highspire's stone. Do you truly believe their fortress can protect your bloodline from what lies beneath?”

You look beyond him towards the distant outline of the garrison.

Highspire's walls are barely visible through the mist, but you know people are sheltering behind them. Families who have lost their homes. Children who have watched the village burn. People who trusted you to help them reach somewhere safe.

You did not come here because you trusted Marek.

You came because the alternative was allowing the truce to collapse before it had a chance to protect anyone.

Marek gestures towards the tent.

“Come inside. We have much to discuss, and I suspect you have considerably more questions than answers.”

The initiates guide you through the entrance.

Inside, the brazier casts an uneven light across the shelves and writing desk. Scrolls are stacked beside sealed jars, and fragments of carved bone rest in carefully arranged trays. A large book lies open beneath a brass weight, its pages covered in intricate silver and black markings.

You recognise the pattern.

It is the same ancient script you encountered beneath Highspire.

Marek follows your gaze.

“Your ancestors left us a remarkable legacy,” he says. “Unfortunately, they also left us a problem that has survived for centuries.”

He turns the book towards you.

“Your bloodline is the missing component.”

You look down at the open pages.

The markings appear to shift slightly as the firelight moves across them. You cannot read the script, but something in your blood seems to recognise its structure. There is a faint pressure behind your eyes, followed by a sensation like a distant heartbeat.

Marek watches your reaction closely.

“Interesting,” he murmurs. “The records were correct. You can sense the old inscriptions without being taught their language.”

He reaches for a narrow strip of parchment.

“That makes you considerably more valuable than you realise, Elara.”

You look up.

“Valuable to whom?”

“For the moment, to me.”

He says it without embarrassment.

Outside, a horn sounds. The soldiers in the camp respond with hurried movement, and someone calls an order near the perimeter. Marek briefly turns towards the entrance, listening.

“The truce will not last indefinitely,” he says. “The Elders want the vault opened. The Fae want it destroyed. Neither side seems particularly concerned with what happens to the people living above it.”

He returns his attention to you.

“I would prefer to understand what we are dealing with before either faction makes an irreversible mistake.”

You cannot tell whether he is being honest.

His words suggest that he sees a distinction between his own intentions and those of the Coven Elders. Yet he has still brought you into an armed encampment, restrained your movements and made it clear that your bloodline is central to his plans.

There may be an opportunity here.

Marek has knowledge you need. He may understand the ancient markings, the foundation anchor and the true purpose of your ancestors' sacrifice. If you can learn enough, you might discover a way to protect Highspire without surrendering control of your bloodline.

But every answer he provides may come with another demand.

You study the open book once more.

The silver markings seem to pulse faintly beneath the surface of the parchment.

Marek waits.

You have two possible approaches. You can challenge his claims, keeping your attention on the magic he uses and the information he reveals. Or you can attempt to negotiate a more permanent arrangement, securing protection for the refugees before agreeing to help him.

Neither option guarantees your safety.

But the next decision may determine whether you remain a prisoner, become a collaborator or find a way to use the Coven's knowledge against it.

choices.text: Hold his stare and defy his authority, clinging to your bond with Balor.
Leverage your knowledge of the Wild path to strike a bargain on Marek's terms.
Challenge his claims and secretly observe how they weave their warding magic.
Attempt to negotiate a permanent pact that spares the village refugees in exchange for your cooperation.

text.content:
The stone beneath your back is colder than the iron oil binding your wrists.

You remain perfectly still on the diagnostic dais, allowing the Coven's warding circles to glow around you. Fine lines of silver and violet light run through the carved grooves in the stone, converging beneath your spine. Every few moments, the markings brighten in response to your heartbeat.
