The magic is searching for something. More accurately, Marek is searching for something through the magic.

You have learned enough about the Coven to recognise that this is not a simple examination. The circles are arranged in overlapping layers, each designed to identify a different aspect of your bloodline. One measures the strength of your ancestral signature. Another traces your connection to the leyline. A third, concealed beneath the dais, appears to be designed to extract whatever power the others discover.

You make a note of its position.

Marek stands beside you, his sleeves rolled neatly to his elbows. His ivory mask rests on a nearby table, leaving his face exposed to the candlelight. Without it, he looks younger than you expected, though the severity of his expression remains unchanged.

“Try not to move,” he says.

“I wasn't aware I had much choice.”

His eyes lift briefly to yours.

“An observation, not a criticism.”

“Then perhaps you should choose your words more carefully.”

For a moment, the corner of his mouth almost moves. He returns his attention to the silver instruments arranged beside the dais.

“Your bloodline has an unusual relationship with the old wards. Most people produce a predictable response. Their magic either resists the leyline or attempts to draw from it. Yours does neither.”

“What does it do?”

“It listens.”

He takes your wrist, turning it gently until your palm faces upwards. His fingers are cool against your skin. A faint silver glow gathers beneath his fingertips, spreading through the veins in your hand.

You feel the familiar pressure of the leyline answering from somewhere deep beneath the camp. It is distant, but not silent. A low vibration travels through your bones, and the markings beneath you brighten.

Marek watches the reaction closely.

“There,” he whispers. “Again.”

You recognise the cadence of his chant now. Three short phrases, followed by a pause, then a fourth phrase spoken in a language that seems to resist being heard. He repeats the sequence, adjusting the final word each time. The magic changes with every variation.

You begin to understand the structure.

The first phrase identifies the bloodline. The second establishes a connection to the leyline. The third attempts to direct that connection through the warding circle. The final phrase should complete the circuit.

But it does not.

There is a deliberate interruption in the final sequence. A safeguard, perhaps, or a restriction imposed by the Elders. The spell is designed to prevent the person being examined from influencing the direction of the magic.

You wonder whether Marek knows it is there.

“Something troubles you,” he says.

“Does it?”

“Your breathing changed.”

“You are examining my pulse, my blood and my breathing. I would have thought that was rather the point.”

He gives you a measured look.

“Most captives are less interested in the details of their examination.”

“Most captives probably haven't spent the last several days listening to Coven scholars explain their work.”

“Have you been listening?”

You turn your wrist slightly within his hand.

“More than you think.”

His expression changes, almost imperceptibly. His attention moves from the silver instruments to your face.

“Then perhaps you can explain what you believe I am doing.”

You could tell him. You could explain that you have recognised the interruption in his chant and that you understand the hidden extraction circle beneath the dais. But knowledge is only useful when it gives you an advantage. For now, you allow him to believe you are simply curious.

“You're trying to establish whether my blood can activate the old wards without opening the vault itself.”

Marek becomes very still.

“And what makes you think that?”

“The second phrase establishes a connection, but the final one never completes it. You're testing the response without allowing the leyline to draw through me.”

His fingers tighten slightly around your wrist.

“That is a remarkably accurate interpretation.”

“Is it?”

“Yes.”

You watch him carefully. He is accustomed to being the person asking questions. You suspect that being understood so quickly is almost as unsettling to him as being challenged.

“Why haven't you completed the sequence?” you ask.

“Because I do not yet know what will happen if I do.”

“Or because the Elders have forbidden you.”

His gaze hardens.

“Be careful.”

There it is. Not anger, exactly. Something closer to caution. You have found a boundary, and he is reminding you that he still has the authority to enforce it.

You let your expression soften.

“I am not trying to provoke you, Marek.”

“That would be a first.”

“Perhaps I am beginning to understand that there is a difference between what you want to discover and what the Coven wants to do with what you discover.”

He looks towards the parchment-covered table. The Sanguine Registers lie open beneath a weighted iron ruler. Their pages contain generations of names, bloodline classifications and records of ancient warding rituals. You have seen enough to understand that your ancestors were not merely imprisoned by the Coven. They were used to maintain the very structures that kept the old powers contained.

Marek follows your gaze.

“You have been reading the registers.”

“I have been reading what you allow me to see.”

“And what conclusion have you reached?”

“That the Coven has mistaken possession for protection.”

His jaw tightens.

“Those records describe a necessary sacrifice. Without the original ward-keepers, the vaults would have opened centuries ago.”

“Perhaps. But the records also describe children being removed from their families, memories being restricted and bloodlines being monitored. Was that necessary too?”

He does not answer immediately.

The silver light beneath your hand fades. Marek releases your wrist, reaching for a small glass instrument. He holds it above your palm, watching the last traces of magic disappear.

“History is rarely as simple as the people who inherit its consequences would like it to be,” he says.

“That does not make it less cruel.”

“No. It does not.”

The admission is quiet, almost unwilling. You study his face. There is no sudden transformation in him, no dramatic rejection of everything he has served. But something has shifted. He is no longer defending the Coven with quite the same certainty.

You decide not to press too hard.

Instead, you allow your fingers to brush his as he places the instrument down.

“You could tell me what you really think,” you say.

“I have told you what I think.”

“You have told me what you can safely say.”

His eyes settle on yours.

For several seconds, neither of you moves. The warding circles continue their slow pulse beneath the dais. You can hear the distant movement of soldiers outside the tent, the scrape of boots against frozen ground and the low murmur of scholars working through the night.

Marek's attention returns to your wrist. His thumb rests against the inside of it, where your pulse beats beneath the skin.

“Your pulse is erratic,” he murmurs. “Either the iron oil is failing... or you are adapting to me.”

You notice that his own breathing has become less regular.

“Which explanation would you prefer?”

“An accurate one.”

“Then perhaps you should stop trying to make me afraid of you.”

His gaze drops briefly to your lips before returning to your eyes.

“Fear is a useful instrument.”

“Useful for whom?”

He says nothing.

You realise that this is the moment you have been waiting for. Not because he has become weak, or because his attraction to you has made him careless, but because he has begun to see the contradiction in his own position. He wants to understand you. He may even want to protect you. Yet every order he follows brings him closer to turning you into the very thing he claims to be studying.

You could exploit that contradiction. You could encourage his growing attachment and use it to gain access to the Council's secrets. But there is a difference between influencing someone and reducing them to another instrument of your survival.

If you want Marek to turn against the Elders, you will need more than a moment of attraction. You will need him to believe that there is a future in which he can stand beside you without surrendering his own judgement.

“Your examination is finished,” he says eventually.

He steps back and begins dismantling the outer warding circle. The iron restraints remain around your wrists, but the pressure of the diagnostic magic recedes.

“Will you tell the Elders what you discovered?” you ask.

“I will tell them that your bloodline remains difficult to classify.”

“That isn't the same as telling them the truth.”

“No,” he replies. “It isn't.”

He gathers the instruments with deliberate care. You watch him place the glass vial containing a trace of your blood inside a locked case. He hesitates before securing it.

“The Council will demand a full demonstration before the next moonrise,” he says. “They will not be satisfied with another diagnostic examination. They will want to see whether you can activate the First Gate.”

“And can I?”

“I don't know.”

“But you suspect I can.”

He looks at you.

“I suspect you can do considerably more than any of us understand.”

The words carry both warning and possibility.

Marek moves towards the tent entrance, then pauses with one hand against the canvas.

“There are things in the registers that the Elders have deliberately concealed. If you intend to survive what comes next, you should know what they are.”

“Why tell me?”

Hs expression becomes difficult to read.

“Perhaps I am tired of being the only person in this camp who knows what we are doing.”

He leaves the tent without another word.

You lie quietly for several moments, listening to the footsteps recede. The warding circles have gone dark, but you can still feel the leyline beneath the stone. It has not forgotten you.

Neither, it seems, has Marek.

You have gained a small measure of trust, though you cannot yet know whether it will be enough to change his allegiance. The Elders have spent generations teaching him that obedience is the same as duty. Breaking that belief will require patience, evidence and a willingness to recognise the parts of him that remain loyal to the Coven.

For now, you have something more useful than affection.

You have his attention.

choices.text: Use your growing intimacy with Marek to slowly draw him away from the Elders' rigid control.

text.content:
The command pavilion is quieter than you expected.

Outside, the Coven's forward camp continues its restless activity. Wardens move between the black-iron perimeter stakes, their armour catching the violet light of the leyline lanterns. Somewhere beyond the canvas walls, a hammer strikes metal in a steady rhythm. Orders are exchanged, horses stamp in the frozen mud, and the distant rumble of the approaching storm occasionally makes the ground tremble beneath your feet.

Inside, Marek's makeshift laboratory is illuminated by a collection of enchanted lanterns suspended from the pavilion's central supports. Their light falls across crowded tables covered in parchment, glass instruments, bone fragments and carefully arranged silver instruments. A large map of the valley occupies the central table, its edges weighted with iron objects to prevent the draughts from disturbing it.

You recognise Highspire almost immediately.

The village is marked in charcoal. The garrison is circled in red ink. Beneath both, a series of faint silver lines traces the leyline network, converging on a point beneath the fortress.

The vault.

Marek stands over the map, his quill moving steadily across a heavily annotated ledger. He has removed his ivory mask, though his expression remains as controlled as ever. His grey eyes move between the pages and the map, measuring distances and calculating possibilities.

“You have been studying the same thing for hours,” you observe.

“Because the answer has not changed.”

“Perhaps you're asking the wrong question.”

His quill stops.

He looks up at you, assessing whether you are about to challenge him or offer something useful.

“And what question should I be asking?”

You approach the table, careful not to disturb the delicate arrangement of silver instruments.

“You want the vault unsealed, Marek,” you say quietly. “And I want my village spared from total destruction. We can reach an accord.”

He does not immediately respond.

Instead, he places his quill down and studies the map. His fingers rest beside the charcoal outline of Highspire, close to the small marks representing the remaining homes and buildings.

“You speak as though those two objectives are naturally compatible.”

“They are if we stop treating each other as obstacles.”

“The vault contains more than ancestral records. It contains a concentration of power that has been deliberately contained for centuries. Unsealing it could destabilise every ward in this valley.”

“And leaving it sealed could mean the Coven continues using my bloodline to maintain it.”

“That is not what I want.”

“Perhaps not. But it is what your Elders want.”

His expression tightens. You have learned that Marek dislikes being reminded of the distance between his own intentions and the institution he serves.

You continue before he can retreat behind another explanation.

“I am not asking you to abandon your research. I am asking you to recognise that I have something to lose as well. My village is not a convenient collection of buildings on your map. Those people have names. They have families, histories and lives that existed long before your soldiers arrived.”

“And if the vault opens?”

“Then we deal with what comes out of it. Together, if you are willing to work with me honestly.”

Marek walks slowly around the table. His coat brushes against the edge of a chair, but he seems not to notice. His attention remains fixed on you.

“You are asking for considerable trust from someone you have every reason to distrust.”

“I am asking for an agreement. Trust can come afterwards.”

A faint, almost imperceptible smile touches his mouth.

“Pragmatic.”

“I have had little opportunity to be anything else.”

He stops in front of you. For a moment, the space between you feels unusually small. The lantern light catches the pale scar running beneath his jaw, a detail you had not noticed before. His expression is still guarded, but there is something less certain behind it.

“You understand that the Council will not accept an informal arrangement,” he says. “They will demand guarantees. They will demand access to the vault, and they will demand that you remain under Coven supervision.”

“Then they can demand.”

“And if they decide that you are no longer useful?”

“That is why I am negotiating with you rather than them.”

His eyes narrow slightly.

“You are placing a great deal of responsibility on my shoulders.”

“You have been carrying the responsibility for this camp since before I arrived. I am simply asking you to decide what you intend to do with it.”

For the first time, he looks away.

His gaze settles on the ledger. Several pages have been marked with small strips of black ribbon. You recognise the family names from the Sanguine Registers, including your own ancestral house. Beside them are columns of figures recording the amount of bloodline resonance required to maintain individual sections of the vault.

Some entries are crossed out.

Others carry notes in Marek's handwriting.

You move closer to examine them.

“What are these?”

“Records of previous warding attempts.”

“And these names?”

“Original custodians.”

“Families like mine?”

He nods.

You scan the entries. The oldest records describe voluntary contributions, but the language changes over time. Later entries refer to compulsory service, hereditary obligation and the removal of children for training. The final columns are particularly disturbing. They record the physical cost of maintaining the wards, including cases where custodians suffered permanent damage.

You look up.

“How many people died?”

Marek's silence is answer enough.

“You knew.”

“I suspected.”

“That isn't the same thing.”

“No,” he says. “It isn't.”

He closes the ledger.

“I have spent years trying to establish whether the original system can be repaired without repeating those practices. The Elders believe the answer is simple. The bloodline must be preserved, the vault must remain controlled, and the custodians must serve.”

“And what do you believe?”

He considers the question.

“I believe that a system which requires generations of unwilling sacrifice is not a system worth preserving.”

The words are spoken quietly, but they carry more weight than any of his earlier explanations.

You study him. It would be easy to mistake this admission for a complete change of heart. It is not. Marek remains a Coven scholar, and he still wants access to the vault. He has not promised to release you, nor has he offered to abandon his position. But he has acknowledged that the Elders' methods may be wrong.

That is something.

“You could help me protect Highspire,” you say.

“And you could help me understand the vault.”

“Then we have the beginnings of an agreement.”

Marek looks down at your hands. He reaches towards you, slowly enough that you could withdraw if you wished. His fingers close around yours with cool, deliberate precision.

“I can offer you something more immediate than a promise.”

From beneath his coat, he produces a heavy iron ring. It is dark, almost black, with a series of intricate runes carved around its outer edge. A small silver mark sits in its centre, shaped like an open eye.

You recognise the design from the sigils worn by the senior Wardens.

“What is it?”

“My personal authority token. It will allow you to pass through the outer Coven lines without being challenged by ordinary patrols. It will not grant you unrestricted access to the command structures, but it should prevent anyone from treating you as an ordinary prisoner.”

He places it in your palm.

The metal is unexpectedly warm.

A faint pulse of magic moves through your fingers. The runes brighten briefly, responding to the blood beneath your skin. You feel the leyline stir somewhere below the pavilion, as though the ring has established a connection between your bloodline and the Coven's warding network.

Marek notices.

“Interesting,” he murmurs. “It has already recognised you.”

You turn the ring over.

“Does everyone know you have given this to me?”

“No.”

“Then why give it to me?”

His gaze holds yours.

“Because if I am going to ask you to work with me, I cannot continue treating you as though you are merely a resource.”

There is something personal in the admission. His thumb brushes lightly across your knuckles before he releases your hand.

“If the Elders see this on you, they will call it treason,” Marek whispers. “Do not prove them right.”

You close your fingers around the ring.

“Are you worried about what they will do to me, or what they will do to you?”

“Both.”

It is the most honest answer he has given you.

For a moment, neither of you speaks. The noise outside seems distant, separated from the pavilion by more than canvas and rope. Marek's gaze lingers on your face, and you wonder whether he is beginning to regret the decision already.

You could press him further. You could ask whether his concern extends beyond the practical value of your bloodline. But you decide against it. Whatever is developing between you remains fragile, and the immediate danger is far more important than forcing him to name it.

Instead, you slip the ring into the inner fold of your tunic.

“Where do we begin?”

Marek returns to the table, though his expression has changed. He unrolls a smaller parchment showing the subterranean structure beneath Highspire Garrison. Several chambers are marked with silver ink, connected by narrow channels that converge on a circular chamber labelled FIRST GATE.

“The vault resonance is strongest here,” he explains. “The original warding system appears to have been designed around three separate anchors. If we can identify their relationship, we may be able to open the First Gate without destabilising the entire network.”

“And if we cannot?”

“Then the Council will attempt a forced opening.”

You look at the map.

“How long?”

“Two days. Perhaps less.”

You absorb the information, studying the channels and their intersections. The ring against your chest feels heavier than it should. You can sense its faint magical pulse against your skin.

Marek hands you a second quill.

“Your bloodline may be able to identify the resonance patterns that my instruments cannot detect. I will need you to work directly with the map.”

You take the quill.

“Then you had better explain everything properly.”

A brief smile returns to his face.

“I was beginning to suspect you would insist.”

As you lean over the table together, the distance between you disappears into the work. He explains the markings, you question his assumptions, and gradually the scattered fragments begin to form a pattern.

You notice something he has overlooked: three of the silver channels do not lead towards the First Gate. They curve away from it, disappearing beneath the western foundations of the garrison.

Marek follows the line with his finger.

“That cannot be right.”

“Why?”

“Those channels should have been sealed centuries ago.”

“Then perhaps they weren't.”

The lanterns flicker.

Beneath the pavilion, the leyline gives a sudden, deep pulse. The ring against your chest responds with a brief flash of violet light.

Marek looks towards the ground.

For the first time that evening, his composure falters.

“Whatever those channels connect to,” he says, “it is still active.”

You exchange a glance.

The agreement between you has barely begun, and already the vault is responding.

You have gained access to the Coven's lines, Marek's confidence and a glimpse of the knowledge the Elders have concealed. But the ring is more than a token of safe passage. It is a connection to the very network you are trying to understand.

If the Council discovers what you are doing, neither of you may be able to undo it.

choices.text: Conceal Marek's sigil in your tunic and begin working alongside him to map the vault resonance.

text.content:
The war room falls quiet as you study the map spread across the commander's table.

Highspire Garrison has stood for centuries, its outer walls built to withstand armies, sieges and the occasional rebellion. But the approaching threat is not an ordinary army. The ash-fog rolling down from the mountains carries something unnatural within it, and the reports from the northern watch suggest that the Coven's forces are already testing the valley's ancient defences.

The senior captains gather around the table. Their armour is marked with mud and soot, and several have the exhausted expressions of men who have spent the night preparing for a battle they do not fully understand.

Commander Vane stands at the head of the table, one hand resting beside the miniature wooden model of the outer gate.

“We have two choices,” he says. “We hold the outer walls and attempt to stop them before they reach the bailey, or we withdraw our primary forces towards the inner keep and prepare for a sustained defence.”

Captain Rusk, a broad-shouldered veteran with a scar running across his cheek, immediately objects.

“Withdraw? We surrender the outer wall and hand them the gate. We should put every available soldier on the battlements and make them pay for every step.”

“And if the battlements fall?” asks another captain.

“Then we fall back.”

“Through what? A gate they will already have broken?”

The disagreement begins to spread around the table. One officer argues for a concentrated defence at the northern entrance. Another suggests sending cavalry through the eastern postern to disrupt the Coven's siege equipment before it reaches the walls.

You examine the map.

The outer gate is strong, but its foundations are old. The stonework has been weakened by years of exposure to the valley's harsh winters. More importantly, the gate is positioned directly above one of the leyline channels you have begun to suspect is connected to the ancient vault beneath the fortress.

If the Coven can manipulate that power, the gate may become a weakness rather than a defence.

You place your hand against the wooden model.

“The outer gate won't hold if their magic is as strong as the rumours say,” you warn the council. “We pull our primary defence back to the inner keep threshold, reinforce the portcullis with double timbers, and choke their advance.”

Captain Rusk turns towards you.

“You're proposing we abandon the outer defences?”

“I'm proposing that we stop pretending stone alone will protect us.”

He looks ready to argue, but Commander Vane raises one hand.

“Explain.”

You move a small wooden marker from the outer gate towards the inner bailey.

“Let them breach the first entrance if they have the power to do it. We make certain they cannot advance quickly once they are inside. The bailey narrows towards the inner arches, which gives us a natural choke point. We reinforce the portcullis, block the secondary passages and place our strongest defenders behind the inner threshold.”

You indicate the surrounding buildings.

“Move the supply wagons out of the central passage. Use them to create barriers along the western approach. Archers can cover the courtyard from the upper windows, while infantry hold the arches. If their forces enter the bailey, they will have to advance through a narrow corridor under constant fire.”

“And the civilians?” Vane asks.

“Move them into the lower keep. The old storage chambers are defensible, provided we clear the entrances and maintain access to the wells.”

Rusk folds his arms.

“And if the Coven simply burns through the inner wall?”

“Then we have lost nothing by preparing a second line of defence. But if we spread our soldiers across every wall and gate, we risk losing them all at once.”

The commander studies the map for several moments.

You can see that he is considering the practical difficulties. Withdrawing soldiers will damage morale. Abandoning the outer wall will look like weakness, and the captains will have to explain to their troops why they are giving ground before the enemy has even arrived.

But the alternative is worse.

“Do it,” Vane says eventually. “We reinforce the inner threshold. Rusk, take two companies and secure the northern approach. I want the portcullis strengthened before nightfall.”

The senior captain looks dissatisfied, but he gives a sharp nod.

“Understood, Commander.”

The meeting breaks apart almost immediately.

Orders are shouted through the corridors, runners are dispatched to the barracks, and the quartermaster begins calculating how much timber and iron can be spared from the stores. Within minutes, the fortress has shifted from argument to action.

You follow Vane into the inner bailey.

The atmosphere is tense but purposeful. Soldiers carry bundles of timber across the courtyard while work crews drag heavy iron braces towards the arches. The sound of hammers echoes against the stone walls. A group of refugees are being escorted towards the lower keep, their belongings piled into carts.

Mara stands beside one of the wagons, holding Elsie's hand. Tomas is helping a pair of soldiers move a damaged supply crate. Their faces brighten when they see you, although the worry in their expressions does not disappear.

Mara approaches.

“They say the outer gate is being abandoned.”

“Not abandoned. We're concentrating the defence further inside.”

“Will it hold?”

You glance towards the inner arches.

“It gives us a better chance.”

She nods, accepting that it is the most honest answer you can offer. Elsie watches the soldiers working, clutching a small piece of cloth in her hand.

You make certain that the refugees are directed towards the lower keep rather than the exposed western storehouses. Then you return to the defensive works.

The inner arches are older than the outer gate. Their stonework is decorated with faded carvings, many of which appear to be part of the original warding system. Some are barely visible beneath layers of dust and mortar.

As the work crews begin fitting the iron braces, you notice something unusual.

A thin line of violet light runs through one of the carvings.

It disappears almost immediately, but you recognise the colour. It is the same unnatural glow that accompanied the destruction of Highspire village.

You crouch beside the stonework.

The carving resembles a series of interlocking circles, with a narrow channel running towards the foundations. It does not look like a conventional defensive marking. It is more likely part of the ancient system beneath the fortress.

A soldier approaches with a hammer.

“Should we cover this section, my lady?”

You hesitate.

If the carving is part of the original warding network, placing iron directly across it could interfere with the magic. But leaving it exposed might allow the Coven to exploit it.

Commander Vane joins you, following your gaze.

“Something wrong?”

“Possibly. These markings may be connected to the old vault. I don't think we should disturb them until we understand what they do.”

He studies the carving.

“Can they help defend the keep?”

“I don't know. But I would rather not destroy something that might be keeping the foundations intact.”

Vane nods and orders the work crew to leave that section untouched. The iron braces are fitted around it instead, preserving the original markings while strengthening the arch.

By late afternoon, the inner threshold has begun to take shape as a defensive position. Timber barriers narrow the approaches, the portcullis has been reinforced, and archers are positioned above the courtyard. The refugees are sheltered below, and the soldiers know where they must stand if the outer gate falls.

It is not a perfect defence. No wall can guarantee safety against an enemy capable of manipulating the magic beneath the ground.

But it is a plan based on what you know, rather than what you hope.

Vane approaches as the last brace is secured.

“You made the right call,” he says. “Rusk won't admit it, but he understands why we need this position.”

“Will the soldiers hold?”

“They will if they know what they're protecting.”

His gaze moves towards the lower keep, where the refugees are being settled.

“You have given them something worth defending.”

A distant horn sounds from the northern watchtower.

The work crews stop. Soldiers turn towards the outer wall, and the violet lanterns along the battlements flicker in unison.

The Coven is approaching.

You look towards the inner arches. Beneath the newly fitted iron braces, the ancient markings give another faint pulse of violet light.

The fortress is ready to receive the attack, but you cannot shake the feeling that its oldest defences are beginning to wake.

choices.text: Supervise the reinforcement of the inner arches and check the defensive seals.

text.content:
The war room is filled with the uneasy murmur of officers waiting for a decision.

A large tactical map covers the commander's table, its edges weighted with iron markers and broken pieces of slate. The northern approach to Highspire is marked in charcoal, showing the narrow road winding between the forest and the rocky slopes. Beyond it, the valley opens into a broad stretch of exposed ground before reaching the outer trench.

You study the positions carefully.

The Coven's forces are still some distance away, but the reports from the watchtowers are becoming increasingly alarming. Scouts have seen enormous shapes moving through the ash-fog. The ground trembles at irregular intervals, and the northern ward-stones have begun to flicker.

Commander Vane stands at the head of the table, listening as Captain Rusk describes the latest sightings.

“Three siege-beasts, possibly more,” Rusk reports. “They are moving behind the vanguard. We cannot see their full size through the fog, but the trees are breaking ahead of them.”

“How far from the trench?” Vane asks.

“An hour, perhaps less.”

Another captain leans forward.

“We should reinforce the gates. If those creatures reach the outer wall, they'll tear through the timber supports.”

“Then we put more men on the walls,” Rusk replies. “Archers, crossbowmen, every available soldier.”

“And let the siege-beasts walk straight towards us?” you ask.

The officers turn towards you.

You move closer to the table, examining the marked positions. Highspire's outer wall is formidable, but its strength depends on the enemy reaching it without first weakening the foundations. The Coven will understand that. If their siege-beasts can batter the wall while the Wardens attack the gates, the defenders will be forced to divide their attention.

You look towards the northern tree line.

There is an opportunity to stop them before they reach the fortress.

You slam your hand down on the tactical map, pointing straight at the outer wall-walk.

“We don't wait for them to break our doors,” you tell Commander Vane and the captains. “We calibrate the cold-iron ballistas now, angle them towards the tree line, and catch their siege-beasts out in the open before they reach the trench.”

For a moment, nobody speaks.

Captain Rusk studies the map, then looks towards the narrow stretch of open ground.

“Those weapons haven't been fired in years,” he says. “The upper ballistas are poorly maintained, and the lower platforms have lost half their counterweights.”

“Then we repair them.”

“And if the bolts fail to penetrate?”

“Then we have spent a few hours preparing weapons that might still slow their advance. If we do nothing, those creatures will reach the walls untouched.”

Commander Vane watches you carefully.

You can see the calculation behind his expression. An aggressive defence carries considerable risk. The ballistas are exposed on the wall-walk, and the soldiers operating them will be among the first targets once the Coven comes within range.

But the potential reward is significant. A successful strike could destroy the siege-beasts before they reach the trench, buying the garrison valuable time.

Vane nods slowly, a fierce grin breaking across his scarred face.

“A bold strike. Let's make them bleed before they touch our stone.”

He turns towards the captains.

“Rusk, take the upper wall. I want every ballista inspected and ready. Send the armourers to the lower platforms. Any weapon that can still turn is to be brought into service.”

The officers begin issuing orders.

Within minutes, the fortress is alive with activity.

You climb the narrow stone staircase towards the northern wall-walk. The wind is bitterly cold, carrying the smell of damp earth and something acrid from the mountains. Below, soldiers are moving crates of ammunition into position while armourers examine the heavy mechanisms.

The ballistas are larger than you expected.

Their wooden frames are reinforced with iron bands, and their thick torsion cords are wound around enormous wooden spools. Each weapon is designed to launch a heavy bolt capable of piercing armour or breaking through a creature's hide.

The bolts themselves are stored beneath canvas coverings. Their iron heads are darkened with a faint silver sheen, and small runes have been etched along the shafts.

Cold iron.

You approach the nearest weapon.

An older armourer named Harlan is crouched beside its firing mechanism, turning a heavy crank with both hands. His grey beard is tied back with a leather cord, and his sleeves are stained with grease.

“You're the one who suggested bringing these back into service?” he asks.

“I am.”

“Then I hope you know what you're asking for. These things are temperamental at the best of times.”

He gestures towards the mechanism.

“The upper crank is slipping. The release catch is stiff, and the aiming gear has seized halfway through its rotation. We can probably get it firing, but I wouldn't trust it to hit anything smaller than the gate.”

You crouch beside him.

“Can we adjust the counterweight?”

“Possibly. But we'll need to release the tension first.”

You examine the arrangement of gears and iron supports. The mechanism is old, but not beyond repair. A small retaining pin has slipped out of its housing, allowing the main crank to move unevenly. You point it out to Harlan.

“That looks like the problem.”

He follows your finger.

“Well, I'll be.”

Together, you work to secure the mechanism. Two soldiers hold the frame steady while Harlan replaces the pin and tightens the retaining bolts. The crank begins to move more smoothly.

A second armourer approaches carrying a long measuring rod.

“We've got another problem,” she says. “The firing angle is too high. If we leave it as it is, the bolts will pass over the trench and strike the forest beyond.”

You look towards the tree line.

The distance is difficult to judge through the drifting ash-fog, but the siege-beasts will have to pass through the exposed ground before reaching the trench. The ballistas need to be angled low enough to strike them there.

“Can we lower the mounting frame?”

“Not without shifting the rear support.”

“Then shift it.”

The armourer gives you a brief, appraising look before calling for additional help.

As the soldiers begin adjusting the frame, you inspect the heavy bolts. Each one is nearly as long as a man, with a broad iron head designed to penetrate thick hide. The runes along the shaft glow faintly when you bring them close to the ballista.

You feel a small answering pulse beneath your skin.

For a moment, the sound of the fortress seems to fade. The cold iron is not merely enchanted metal. It carries a faint resonance, something designed to disrupt the magic of whatever it strikes.

You realise why the Coven's forces might fear these weapons.

If the siege-beasts are sustained by leyline magic, a well-placed bolt could do more than wound them. It might interrupt the power keeping them alive.

You mention this to Harlan.

He looks at the bolt, then back at you.

“That's what the old inscriptions suggest. These weapons were built during the first wars against the things that came out of the vaults.”

“Then they were designed for this.”

“Perhaps. But nobody has fired one in living memory.”

You look towards the mountains.

“That makes today a good day to start.”

A low horn sounds from the northern tower.

Every soldier on the wall turns towards the valley.

Through the drifting fog, you can just make out movement between the trees. Something enormous shifts behind the branches. A second shape follows it, and then a third. The tops of the trees bend and snap as the creatures force their way through the forest.

The siege-beasts are coming.

Commander Vane appears beside you, his cloak snapping in the wind.

“How many weapons are ready?”

“Four on the northern wall. Two more should be operational within the hour.”

“Enough to make a difference?”

You look at the enormous bolts resting beside the firing frames.

“If the crews can hold their aim.”

Vane follows your gaze.

“Then make certain they do.”

He orders the soldiers into position. The ballista crews take their places, loading the first bolts into the firing channels. Archers spread along the parapet, while infantry form defensive lines behind the stone battlements.

You walk along the wall, checking each mechanism and ensuring the crews understand their firing angles. The soldiers listen carefully. Some look frightened, but there is a growing confidence among them. They have something more than a wall to hide behind now. They have a chance to strike first.

Below, you hear voices calling your name.

Several villagers have gathered near the courtyard entrance, watching the preparations. Tomas raises one hand in greeting. Mara stands beside him, keeping Elsie close. Their presence reminds you that the battle is not simply about military positions or the survival of the fortress.

It is about the people behind you.

The people who trusted you when you stood in the village square. The people who followed you towards Highspire because you promised there was somewhere they might survive.

You turn back towards the valley.

The first siege-beast emerges from the tree line.

It is enormous, its body covered in dark, ridged armour that resembles the bark of an ancient tree. Violet light pulses between the plates along its spine. Its head is low to the ground, and two heavy limbs drag through the soil as it advances.

A second creature follows, carrying a structure of twisted bone and black iron across its back.

The ballista crews begin turning their cranks.

Commander Vane draws his sword.

“Hold until they reach the open ground,” he orders. “Then fire.”

You take your position beside the nearest ballista, watching the creatures approach.

The first bolt is ready.

The fortress holds its breath.

choices.text: Inspect the calibration cranks on the wall-walk and prepare the heavy bolts.

text.content:
The wind coming down from Frost-Spire Ridge is sharp enough to make your eyes water.

You lie flat against the frozen moss, one arm tucked beneath your chest and the other gripping a narrow ledge of rock. Below you, the valley floor disappears beneath a shifting blanket of grey ash-fog. It moves in slow, unnatural currents, curling around the trees and gathering in the hollows between the rocks.

You have been watching the Coven's advance for nearly an hour.

At first, you saw only movement: dark shapes passing between the trees, the occasional flash of iron armour and the faint violet glow of their warding lanterns. Now the fog has thinned enough to reveal the scale of the force moving through the valley.

This is not a scouting party.

The Coven's entire war-host is marching towards Highspire.

Rows of armoured Wardens advance along the old northern road, their black cloaks snapping in the wind. Behind them come supply wagons reinforced with iron plates, followed by ranks of initiates carrying staffs and bundles of bone charms. The wagons are pulled by enormous creatures whose bodies seem assembled from twisted branches, animal remains and pale, exposed bone.

You recognise the siege-beasts from the earlier reports.

Their heavy limbs crush the frozen earth as they move. Violet light pulses beneath their armour, illuminating the ash that gathers around their feet. Each step sends a faint tremor through the ridge.

You shift slightly, trying to find a better view.

The movement brings you dangerously close to the edge. A small stone breaks free beneath your elbow and tumbles down the slope.

You freeze.

It bounces twice before disappearing into the fog.

One of the Wardens stops.

He raises his head towards the ridge, his face concealed behind a narrow iron mask. A second soldier turns to follow his gaze.

You press yourself against the rock and barely breathe.

The Warden watches the hillside for several seconds before a captain calls to him from below. He turns away, and the column continues moving.

You wait until the sound of their footsteps has swallowed the small noise you made.

You cannot afford to be discovered. If the Coven captures you here, Highspire will lose its warning, and you will have no way of knowing whether the garrison has prepared for what is coming.

You begin studying the formation more carefully.

The first thing you notice is that the war-host is not arranged as a single advancing force. Its divisions are separated by deliberate gaps, each positioned to serve a different purpose.

The siege-beasts are travelling towards the western side of the valley, where the ground is flatter and the approach to Highspire's outer gate is least obstructed. Their route is marked by small bone standards planted at regular intervals.

Behind them, a group of Wardens carries long poles wrapped in dark cloth. Every few minutes, they stop and drive the poles into the earth. A faint violet pulse travels outwards from each one, spreading beneath the ground before fading.

You recognise the technique.

They are testing the leyline.

The Coven is not simply choosing the easiest route to the fortress. It is identifying the weakest points in the ancient network beneath it.

You follow the line of their progress with your eyes.

Near the centre of the column, several captains ride beneath a canopy of black branches. Each carries a bone staff decorated with silver rings. They communicate through a series of precise gestures, raising or lowering their staffs to direct the different divisions.

You begin memorising the signals.

A raised staff followed by a slow turn appears to indicate a change in direction. Two rapid movements send a smaller group towards the eastern edge of the road. A staff held horizontally brings the supply wagons to a halt.

You watch one captain repeat the sequence.

The eastern group separates from the main force.

Unlike the soldiers surrounding them, these figures wear no visible armour. Their clothing is dark and closely fitted, with strips of pale material wrapped around their forearms. Each carries an obsidian tool or a narrow iron staff.

Ward-breakers.

You have heard the name before, though nobody at Highspire has explained exactly what they do.

Now you begin to understand.

They are not being sent to attack the walls.

They are heading towards the lower slopes beneath the fortress, following a route that disappears behind a line of ancient standing stones. Their equipment is designed for working against the foundations rather than fighting soldiers.

You move your gaze towards the garrison.

Highspire's walls rise above the valley, their towers visible through the thinning fog. From this distance, the fortress looks almost invulnerable. But you know that its strength is partly an illusion. The old vault beneath it is connected to the stonework, and the ancient wards run through the foundations.

If the ward-breakers can reach those channels, they may be able to undermine the entire defensive system without ever approaching the gate.

The real attack is going to happen in two places at once.

You study the captains again.

One of them dismounts beside a large map spread across the bonnet of a supply wagon. He places a bone marker on the western gate, then another beneath the fortress. A third marker is placed near the northern watchtower.

The captain speaks to the others. Although you cannot hear the words, you watch their reactions.

One points towards the western approach. Another gestures beneath the fortress. The final captain raises his staff, and the surrounding Wardens move into formation.

You piece together the plan.

The siege-beasts will strike the western gate, forcing the garrison to concentrate its soldiers along the outer wall. While the defenders are occupied, the ward-breakers will attack the subterranean foundations. Their objective is likely to disrupt the ancient defensive seals, weakening the fortress from below and allowing the main force to enter.

A simultaneous attack from above and beneath.

It is a carefully constructed plan, designed to exploit the garrison's assumption that the greatest threat will come from the visible army.

You reach for the small scrap of parchment tucked inside your coat. Keeping your movements slow, you sketch the positions of the main divisions and mark the route taken by the ward-breakers.

Your fingers are stiff with cold, and the charcoal keeps threatening to snap.

You record everything you can remember: the number of siege-beasts, the position of the supply wagons, the captains' signalling system and the likely location of the subterranean assault.

You also mark the bone standards.

They appear to form a loose line between the forest and the western gate. If the Coven is using them to guide the siege-beasts or reinforce their magic, destroying them might disrupt the advance.

You cannot be certain, but it is worth telling Vane.

A sudden movement below draws your attention.

One of the ward-breakers has stopped near the standing stones. He kneels and places an obsidian tool against the ground. A thin violet line spreads outwards from the point of contact, travelling through the frozen earth.

For an instant, the ridge beneath you vibrates.

The stone under your hand feels warm.

You pull away instinctively.

A faint whisper moves through the rock, too low to understand but strangely familiar. The sensation travels up your arm and settles beneath your ribs, where your bloodline seems to answer it.

The ward-breaker looks towards the ridge.

You remain perfectly still.

His head tilts slightly, as though he has heard something that the others cannot. He raises one hand, and the violet line beneath him brightens.

Then a captain calls from the road.

The ward-breaker withdraws his tool. The light fades, and he rejoins the others.

You look down at your hand.

A faint silver mark has appeared across your palm, but it disappears almost as soon as you notice it.

Whatever the Coven is doing beneath the fortress, the ancient network is responding to your presence.

You cannot investigate it now.

The war-host has begun moving again, and the distance between its scouts and your position is narrowing. A pair of Wardens have separated from the main column and are making their way towards the lower ridge. They may simply be checking the perimeter, but you cannot risk waiting to find out.

You carefully fold the parchment and secure it inside your coat.

The intelligence you have gathered is more valuable than any weapon you could carry. Highspire needs to know that the western gate is only a distraction, and that the real danger lies beneath the fortress.

You begin withdrawing along the ridge.

The descent is steep, and the frozen ground makes every step dangerous. You avoid the exposed trail, choosing a narrow route between two outcrops where the rocks provide cover from the valley below.

Behind you, the Coven's war-host continues its advance.

A horn sounds from the western column. Another answers from the eastern edge of the forest. The siege-beasts turn towards the fortress, their violet-lit bodies emerging from the fog like enormous moving shadows.

You pause once to look back.

The Wardens are already establishing their forward positions. Their bone standards are being driven into the ground, and the ward-breakers have disappeared beneath the northern slope.

The attack is closer than you thought.

You need to reach Highspire before the first assault begins.

As you continue down the ridge, you rehearse the information you will give Commander Vane. The siege-beasts will strike the western gate. The ward-breakers will target the foundations. The Coven's captains are coordinating both attacks through their bone staffs, and the standards may be reinforcing their advance.

For once, the enemy's intentions are not hidden behind rumour or speculation.

You know what they are planning.

Whether the garrison can use that knowledge in time is another matter.

The fortress comes into view below you, its walls catching the last pale light of the afternoon. Soldiers are already moving along the battlements, preparing for an attack they may not yet understand.

You quicken your pace.

Highspire has a chance to survive this assault, but only if its defenders know where the real battle will be fought.

choices.text: Slip away quietly down the ridge trail to carry this intelligence back to Highspire.

text.content:
The narrow gorge offers the perfect place to stop an advancing army.

Steep rock walls rise on either side of the frozen trail, their upper ledges crowded with twisted pine trees and shelves of frost-shattered shale. The path below is barely wide enough for three soldiers to march abreast. Beyond the gorge, the valley opens towards Highspire, but any force attempting to reach the fortress must first pass through this natural bottleneck.

You have spent the better part of an hour preparing the ambush.

Heavy pine logs have been wedged between the rocks above the trail, secured with ropes and wooden supports. Loose shale has been gathered into unstable piles, ready to be dislodged by the smallest disturbance. You have also positioned several smaller rocks along the upper ledge, giving you a secondary means of disrupting the advance if the first attack fails.

It is dangerous work.

The ground is slippery, the wind is bitter, and one mistake could send you tumbling into the gorge before the Coven soldiers ever arrive.

But you have no intention of allowing them an easy passage.

You crouch behind a cluster of frozen boulders, watching the trail below.

The first signs of movement appear through the mist.

A dark figure emerges between the trees, followed by another. Their armour is blackened with iron, and pale bone charms hang from their belts. They move cautiously, stopping every few steps to examine the ground.

Scouts.

You count six before the main force appears.

Behind them comes a larger group of Wardens, carrying long staffs and shields marked with the Coven's silver sigil. Their movements are disciplined, their formation tight. At the centre of the column, several figures carry obsidian torches that burn with a strange violet flame.

You recognise the equipment from the earlier reports.

Ward-breakers.

They are not ordinary soldiers. Their tools are designed to disrupt the ancient protective magic beneath Highspire. If they reach the fortress, they could undermine its defences without ever having to breach the walls.

You watch their formation carefully.

Two Wardens lead the column, with the ward-breakers protected in the middle. The remaining soldiers form a rear guard, ensuring that nobody can approach from behind.

They are expecting an attack from the fortress.

They are not expecting one from above.

You glance towards the ropes securing the pine logs. They are stretched tight, their fibres creaking under the weight of the timber. A single pull on the signal string will release the first support. The logs will roll down the slope, carrying the loose shale with them.

The resulting avalanche should bury the narrow trail.

You take a slow breath.

The first Warden reaches the centre of the gorge.

Then the second.

The ward-breakers follow, their obsidian torches casting flickering shadows across the rock walls.

You wait until the entire lead formation is beneath the prepared slope.

A moment longer.

The rear guard begins to enter the gorge.

Now.

You loose the signal string.

For a fraction of a second, nothing happens.

Then the upper supports give way.

An enormous pine log tears free from the ledge, crashing into the slope below. A second follows, then a third. The frozen earth breaks apart beneath them, sending a mass of shale and broken branches thundering down the gully walls.

The noise is deafening.

The first Warden looks up just in time to see the avalanche descending.

He shouts a warning, but the sound is swallowed by the collapsing hillside.

The logs strike the trail with tremendous force. One smashes into the front of the formation, throwing two soldiers against the rock wall. Another rolls directly through the ward-breakers, scattering their obsidian torches across the frozen ground.

The shale follows.

A wave of broken stone and ice sweeps through the narrow gorge, burying the lower half of the trail. Two of the ward-breakers disappear beneath the debris, while their escorts are thrown into the snow and tangled branches.

You grip the rock beside you as the ground shakes.

The impact sends a sharp vibration through the ridge. Smaller stones break loose around your position, tumbling into the gorge. One strikes the boulder beside your head and splits into several pieces.

You duck.

For several seconds, the entire world seems to be moving.

Then the avalanche settles.

The gorge is almost unrecognisable.

The Coven's lead formation has been shattered. Soldiers struggle beneath fallen timber, while others attempt to drag their companions clear of the debris. One of the obsidian torches lies broken against the rocks, its violet flame flickering weakly before disappearing beneath the snow.

You have done it.

The vanguard is no longer advancing.

A sudden cry rises from below.

A surviving Warden has managed to stand. His shield is cracked, and blood runs down one side of his face. He looks towards the ridge, searching for whoever caused the destruction.

You flatten yourself against the rocks.

He raises his staff.

A pulse of violet light spreads across the gorge, illuminating the fallen trees. The Warden is attempting to locate the source of the disturbance through the surrounding leyline.

You feel the magic brush against your skin.

For a moment, your blood responds.

The faint pressure beneath your ribs becomes a sharp, almost painful vibration. You press one hand against the frozen earth, trying to steady yourself. The Warden's magic moves past your position, but you are left with the uncomfortable sensation that something beneath the mountain has noticed you.

The surviving Coven soldiers begin to regroup.

One captain climbs onto a fallen log and raises his bone staff. He gives a series of sharp signals, directing the remaining Wardens to establish a defensive perimeter.

Another soldier begins examining the debris.

You watch as he kneels beside one of the buried ward-breakers. The figure is motionless, their obsidian tools scattered across the trail. The soldier calls for help, but the captain orders him to leave the body and secure the ridge instead.

They have lost men, equipment and valuable time.

But they have not been destroyed.

A horn sounds from somewhere beyond the gorge.

The note carries across the valley, long and low. A second horn answers from further north, followed by a third from the direction of the main Coven column.

Your stomach tightens.

The rest of the war-host has heard the avalanche.

You look towards the ridge behind you. Through a break in the mist, you can see movement along the distant slopes. Dark figures are turning towards the gorge, and several violet lights begin moving away from the main road.

The Coven knows exactly where you are.

You have bought Highspire time, but you have also revealed your position to an enemy with considerably more soldiers than you can fight alone.

A bolt strikes the rock above your head.

The impact sends fragments of stone scattering across your shoulders.

You turn towards the source.

A Coven archer has reached the lower slope. He is pointing towards your position, shouting to the others. Two more soldiers raise their weapons.

You move immediately.

Keeping low, you scramble towards the narrow trail leading away from the gorge. The ground is uneven, and the mist makes it difficult to judge the distance between the rocks. Behind you, another bolt strikes the ledge, sending a shower of frost into the air.

You reach the first outcrop and crouch behind it.

A second later, a Warden appears on the opposite side of the trail.

He has abandoned his shield and carries a short iron blade. His face is streaked with dirt, and his eyes widen when he sees you.

For a moment, neither of you moves.

Then he lunges.

You throw yourself sideways as the blade strikes the rock where your shoulder had been. The impact sends a spark across the stone. You grab a loose branch from the ground and swing it towards his arm, forcing him to stumble.

He recovers quickly.

You cannot afford to fight him here. More soldiers are approaching, and the ridge offers little protection if they surround you.

You kick loose a handful of shale.

The stones scatter beneath his feet, and he loses his balance. You use the moment to scramble past him, climbing towards the upper trail.

A shout follows you.

You do not look back.

The ridge becomes steeper as you climb. Your lungs burn in the cold air, and your hands are scraped from gripping the frozen rock. The physical effort is exhausting, but you keep moving.

You have no intention of being captured after coming this far.

At the top of the slope, you find a narrow trail winding through the pines. The mist is thicker here, concealing the path from the valley below. You pause long enough to listen.

The horns continue.

The Coven's war-host is reorganising, and the vanguard you struck will not be able to advance quickly. The siege-beasts may need to find another route, and the ward-breakers will have to replace the equipment lost in the gorge.

Every minute matters.

You look back once.

The avalanche has transformed the gorge into a wall of timber and shattered stone. The surviving Wardens are gathering beneath the cliffs, but their formation is broken. One of the captains is pointing towards the ridge, directing a search party into the trees.

You have made them bleed before they reached Highspire.

Now you need to make certain the garrison can use the time you have bought.

You begin following the high mist trail towards the western ridge, where the garrison scouts were last reported. They will need to know what happened in the gorge, how many ward-breakers were caught in the avalanche and how quickly the Coven is likely to recover.

The knowledge could change the battle.

As you disappear into the trees, you feel the faint vibration of the leyline beneath your feet. It is stronger than before, almost as though the mountain itself is responding to the violence above it.

You do not know whether the avalanche has disturbed something ancient or whether your own bloodline is reacting to the magic in the fallen ward-breakers' tools.

Either way, the Coven is not the only thing moving beneath these mountains.

You tighten your cloak and continue towards Highspire.

The enemy knows where you are, but it does not yet know what you have accomplished.

That advantage will not last long.

choices.text: Pull back into the high mist trails to regroup with the garrison scouts.

text.content:
The lower bailey is a confusion of activity.

Soldiers hurry between the barracks and the outer walls, carrying crates of ammunition and bundles of timber. Refugees crowd beneath the covered walkways, trying to keep out of the freezing drizzle. Somewhere nearby, a child is crying, while the quartermaster shouts instructions to a group of exhausted labourers.

You watch the movement for several minutes.

The garrison is preparing for a siege, but its resources are limited. The soldiers are trained, armed and organised, yet there are simply not enough of them to defend every entrance, protect the refugees and maintain the ancient wards beneath the fortress.

The villagers could help.

Many have already volunteered to carry supplies, repair barricades and assist the wounded. Some have experience hunting, farming or working with tools. They understand the surrounding countryside better than most of the soldiers stationed here.

But they have very few weapons.

You have seen the militia gathering near the lower courtyard. Tomas has been helping organise the stronger villagers, while several former hunters have offered to patrol the perimeter. They are willing to fight, but willingness alone will not stop a Coven Warden carrying a cold-iron blade.

The reserve armory might contain what they need.

You slip past the wet canvas tents and descend the slippery stone steps into the lower keep cellars. The air becomes colder as you move underground, carrying the smell of damp stone, old leather and rusting metal. The noise of the bailey fades behind you, replaced by the occasional drip of water from the ceiling.

At the bottom of the staircase stands a heavy oak door reinforced with iron bands. A single tallow candle sputters in a wall bracket, providing just enough light to illuminate the carved quartermaster's seal above the lock.

The door is barred.

Through the iron grate, you can see racks of cold-iron spearheads, heavy oak shields and crates of black-feathered arrows. There are also several crossbows, bundles of bowstrings and a collection of smaller weapons stored in wooden cases.

Exactly what the refugee militia needs.

You step closer to examine the lock.

A stoic garrison guard stands at the foot of the stairs, one hand resting on the pommel of their sword. Their armour is clean but worn, and their expression suggests that they have been given very clear instructions about who is permitted to enter.

“Keep area is restricted to military personnel, villager,” the guard says neutrally. “Return to the bailey.”

You glance towards the armory.

“I need to speak to the quartermaster.”

“Then you can speak to him in the bailey.”

“He is not there.”

“That is unfortunate.”

The guard makes no effort to move aside.

You recognise that simply demanding access will achieve very little. The garrison has its own command structure, and the guard is unlikely to risk disobeying an order because a village leader has decided that the militia needs weapons.

You need to find another way.

Your attention moves towards the lock. You instantly recognise the quartermaster's seal on the door, knowing the latch bolt can be manipulated with a thin piece of iron wire. The mechanism is old-fashioned but well made, and you can already see where the internal catch must sit. Given a few uninterrupted moments, you could probably open it without damaging the door.

You study the sentry's posture. Their shoulders are beginning to sag, and they favour their left foot slightly. Fatigue has made them less alert than they would like to appear. Their attention keeps drifting towards the commotion above, where another argument has broken out near the supply wagons. You suspect that a sufficiently well-timed distraction could give you the opportunity to reach the lock.

You consider your position among the refugees. Mara, Tomas and the other villagers know you, and several have already followed your decisions during the evacuation. Your reputation as a village leader may not carry much weight with the garrison, but the soldiers have seen how the refugees respond to you. Perhaps you can use that influence to negotiate access for the militia.

You look back at the guard.

“How many soldiers are available to defend the lower bailey?”

The question seems to catch them off guard.

“That's not your concern.”

“It becomes my concern when the people sheltering here are left without protection.”

“The garrison will defend the refugees.”

“With how many soldiers?”

The guard's expression hardens.

“Enough.”

You look past them towards the stairs.

Above, boots thunder across the stone floor. Someone calls for additional men at the northern gate. Another voice answers that the upper wall is already short of archers.

The guard hears it too.

You return your attention to the door.

“The soldiers cannot defend every corridor and every refugee shelter. You know that as well as I do.”

For a moment, the guard says nothing.

Then they glance towards the armory.

“Those weapons are reserved for the garrison.”

“And what happens when the garrison runs out of soldiers?”

The question hangs between you.

You are not asking the guard to abandon their responsibilities. You are asking them to recognise that the people sheltering behind these walls may have to defend themselves. If the Coven breaches the outer defences, the refugees will not be protected simply because they have been told to remain in the lower keep.

The guard shifts their weight.

“I would need an order from the quartermaster.”

“Then take me to him.”

“He is overseeing the eastern stores.”

“Then tell him I am waiting.”

The guard hesitates.

You notice a small change in their expression. They are not convinced, but they are beginning to consider the possibility that refusing you may be more dangerous than allowing you to speak with the quartermaster.

Before they can answer, a crash echoes from above.

The guard turns sharply towards the staircase.

A moment later, a young soldier comes running down, carrying a broken shield.

“The northern stores have been hit by falling debris,” he reports breathlessly. “Captain Rusk wants additional equipment moved to the upper wall.”

The guard swears under their breath.

You seize the opportunity.

“If the upper wall needs weapons, then the reserve armory needs to be opened. Let the quartermaster decide what can be spared, but the militia cannot remain unarmed while everyone else prepares for battle.”

The guard looks between you and the soldier.

Finally, they reach for the keys.

“Wait here. I will speak to the quartermaster.”

They unlock the outer fastening but leave the inner bar in place.

It is a small concession, but it gives you a chance to see inside.

The armory is larger than you expected. Wooden racks line the walls, with weapons arranged according to type and condition. Several crates have been opened recently, revealing bundles of spearheads wrapped in oiled cloth. Along the far wall, a collection of shields bears the faded insignia of an earlier garrison.

You count at least twenty serviceable weapons.

Enough to equip a small militia.

The guard returns several minutes later, accompanied by an older man wearing a leather apron and carrying a ledger.

The quartermaster looks you up and down.

“I understand you want weapons for the villagers.”

“I do.”

“They are not soldiers.”

“They are people who will be caught in the fighting whether they carry weapons or not.”

He studies you for a moment.

“And you think giving them cold iron will make them useful?”

“I think giving them the means to defend themselves is better than leaving them helpless.”

He glances towards the open armory.

“The garrison has priority. I cannot empty these stores.”

“I am not asking you to.”

You point towards the racks of spearheads and shields.

“Give the militia enough to protect the lower bailey and the refugee shelters. Keep the better equipment for the trained soldiers. We can use the older shields and spare spears.”

The quartermaster considers this.

“Who will organise them?”

“I will.”

He looks towards the guard.

“Have you seen the villagers gathering near the supply wagons?”

The guard nods.

“Some of them have been helping the labourers.”

“Then they can help here too. But I will not have weapons distributed without proper records.”

He opens his ledger.

You agree to help him record every weapon issued and identify which villagers are capable of using bows, spears and crossbows. It is not an ideal arrangement, but it gives the militia a legitimate supply of equipment without stripping the garrison of its best weapons.

As the armory door opens fully, you feel a faint vibration beneath your feet.

The cold-iron weapons seem to respond to something in the stonework. A low hum passes through the racks, barely audible beneath the clatter of metal and the quartermaster's instructions.

You glance towards the floor.

There are old markings carved into the stone beneath the central weapon rack. They are partly obscured by dust, but you recognise the same circular pattern you saw near the inner arches.

The ancient warding system runs through the armory too.

You make a mental note to tell Vane.

For now, there is work to do.

You begin organising the weapons, separating those suitable for the militia from those that require repair. The quartermaster assigns two soldiers to help, and within minutes the first bundles are being carried towards the lower bailey.

When you return to the courtyard, Tomas is waiting beside the supply wagons.

His expression changes when he sees the spearheads.

“Where did those come from?”

“The reserve armory.”

He raises an eyebrow.

“Did they simply give them to you?”

“Not exactly.”

A brief smile crosses his face.

You explain how the weapons will be distributed and which villagers should receive them. Tomas immediately begins gathering the volunteers, while Mara helps identify those who can assist with the wounded and those who should remain with the children.

The militia is beginning to take shape.

It is not an army, and you cannot pretend that a few dozen armed villagers will defeat the Coven. But they can defend the shelters, protect supply routes and prevent panic from spreading if the fighting reaches the bailey.

More importantly, they will not be entirely dependent on the soldiers for their survival.

You look towards the northern walls.

The distant horns have begun again.

The attack is coming, and the fortress will need every advantage it can find.

You have secured weapons for the militia, but you have also discovered that the ancient warding network extends beneath the armory. Whatever is happening beneath Highspire, the fortress is beginning to respond to the approaching Coven.

You will need to understand those markings before the battle reaches the lower keep.

choices.text: Convince the guard that arming the civilians protects the garrison.
Distract the sentry and quietly bypass the lock to distribute weapons.

text.content:
"Listen to me!"

Your voice cuts through the crying and the drum of cold drizzle, steady and unyielding. For a moment, nobody responds. The courtyard remains a confusion of frightened faces, soaked blankets and overturned carts. A child is wailing somewhere near the well. An elderly man sits against the stable wall, one hand pressed to his chest while his daughter tries to shelter him beneath a torn cloak.

You climb onto a heavy grain crate, gripping its damp edge to steady yourself.

"Listen!"

This time, the sharpness in your voice catches their attention.

"Panic will kill us faster than any siege-beast. We have walls around us, supplies in the keep and enough people here to make a difference. But not if everyone stands around waiting for someone else to tell them what to do."

A few faces turn towards you. Others remain lowered, exhausted by grief and fear.

You point towards the eastern side of the bailey, where the stone wall bends inward and offers some protection from the worst of the wind.

"We set up triage tents there. Anyone with medical knowledge works with the injured. Anyone who can carry water brings it from the well. We need dry timber beneath canvas, and the children must be kept together, away from the gates."

A woman near the carts raises her hand.

"What about the wounded? There are more coming from the village."

"Then we make room for them."

"And food?" someone else calls. "We've barely had anything since yesterday."

"We'll deal with that too. But first, we make sure people are warm enough to survive the night."

You look across the courtyard, forcing yourself to meet their eyes.

"Find something useful to do. If you cannot lift a cart, carry a blanket. If you cannot carry anything, help someone who is frightened. Nobody is useless here."

For a heartbeat, the courtyard remains still.

Then Mara steps forward.

Her hair is damp beneath her shawl, and her face is pale with exhaustion. Elsie stands beside her, clutching the edge of her mother's coat. The little girl looks healthier than she did during the fever, but the events of the last few days have left her unusually quiet.

"I can help with the wounded," Mara says. "I've still got some of my supplies. Not much, but enough to start."

"Good. Take the eastern wall."

Tomas appears from behind a loaded cart, carrying two buckets in one hand.

"I can organise the timber," he says. "There are spare planks in the wagon yard. Half of them need repairing, but they'll do for a barricade."

"Then get them under cover before they soak through."

The instructions begin to spread. People who had been standing helplessly in the rain find themselves moving with purpose. Two young men begin dragging carts towards the wall. An older woman gathers the children and leads them towards a sheltered corner beneath the granary awning. Someone finds a stack of old blankets, and another person starts dividing the available firewood into smaller piles.

The courtyard changes by degrees.

It is still cold. It is still frightened. But it is no longer helpless.

You climb down from the crate and begin helping Mara establish a makeshift treatment area. A wagon is turned onto its side to block the wind, and several villagers stretch canvas across its frame. The first injured arrive before the shelter is finished: a boy with a deep cut along his forearm, a farmer whose ankle has swollen badly, and a woman with a burn across her shoulder.

You kneel beside them, working through what can be treated and what must wait.

Your experience makes the decisions easier. You recognise the signs of shock, know how to clean the boy's wound and can distinguish the farmer's painful sprain from something more serious. Mara follows your instructions without hesitation, and soon the treatment area has a workable rhythm.

You turn the overturned wagon into a more secure shelter, using spare rope and broken harness fittings to keep the canvas from collapsing. You also find a way to brace the damaged wheel, giving the injured a stable surface to sit on. The practical work steadies your thoughts, even as the sounds of the wounded continue around you.

You assess the courtyard as you work, noticing which paths remain clear and where people are most likely to become trapped if the gates are breached. You direct the strongest villagers towards moving the heavier carts, keeping the central route open for anyone carrying the wounded. Your instincts tell you that an orderly retreat may become necessary before the night is over.

A familiar voice calls your attention from the far side of the shelter.

"You're going to wear yourself out before they've even reached the walls."

You turn.

Your companion is working tirelessly among the villagers, distributing dry blankets and helping reinforce the outer barricades. Their cloak is soaked through, and a smear of mud runs along one cheek. They have clearly been working for some time.

They catch your eye and offer a brief, reassuring smile. There is no need for either of you to explain why you are here. They know what Highspire means to you, and you know they would have come even if you had ordered them to stay behind.

They pass a blanket to an elderly woman before returning to the barricade.

"You should eat something," they say as they pass you. "You can't organise an entire bailey on an empty stomach."

"Watch me."

"I have been watching you for years. That's precisely why I'm worried."

You almost smile, but the expression fades when a horn sounds from somewhere above the courtyard.

Every conversation stops.

The guards on the inner wall move towards the battlements. One raises a hand to signal another, and a third disappears through a narrow doorway leading into the keep. You follow their movements, trying to judge whether the sound means an approaching attack or simply another report from the scouts.

A moment later, a young soldier descends the steps.

"Commander Vane wants a report on the courtyard."

He looks at the organised treatment area, the stacked timber and the villagers working beneath the canvas.

"Is this your doing?"

You glance towards Mara, Tomas and the others.

"Theirs," you reply. "I only told them where to start."

The soldier studies the courtyard again. His expression changes slightly.

"Captain Rusk said the refugees would be impossible to organise."

"Then perhaps Captain Rusk should spend less time talking about them and more time helping."

The soldier looks as though he might laugh, but thinks better of it.

"Commander Vane will want to hear that."

He turns and hurries back towards the keep.
