You watch him go, aware that the work has attracted more attention than you intended. The villagers are beginning to look towards you whenever another problem arises. Some expect instructions. Others simply seem relieved that somebody is willing to make decisions.

That carries its own responsibility.

A small boy approaches, holding a wooden cup.

"There's water," he says. "Mum told me to bring it to you."

You accept it and drink. The water is cold enough to make your teeth ache.

"Thank you. What's your name?"

"Peter."

"Well, Peter, you've done an important job. Can you take another cup to Mara?"

He nods and hurries away.

You look across the bailey. The shelters are beginning to hold. The wounded have somewhere to lie, the children are gathered together, and the villagers have established a rough system for sharing the available supplies. It is not enough to make anyone safe, but it is a beginning.

The garrison has walls, weapons and trained soldiers. Yet the people inside those walls are frightened, hungry and increasingly aware that the coming siege may not distinguish between soldier and civilian.

You have managed to give them something they were missing: a reason to work together.

Now you must decide what to do with that influence.

The quartermaster's storehouse sits near the inner gate, guarded by two soldiers. You can see sacks of grain being unloaded through its narrow entrance. There are enough supplies to feed the garrison, but you have no idea how much has been allocated to the refugees. A delegation might force the officers to acknowledge the problem before people begin going hungry.

Beyond the storehouse, the lower wooden gates remain exposed. They were built for ordinary traffic, not a siege. Reinforcing them would give the courtyard another line of defence, but it would require tools, timber and people willing to stand in danger.

You look back at the villagers.

They are waiting to see what you will do next.

choices.text: Lead a delegation of organized villagers to demand extra rations.
Form a civilian defensive squad to fortify the lower wooden gates.

text.content:
By late afternoon, the lower bailey of Highspire Garrison has become almost unrecognisable.

The courtyard that had been filled with frightened refugees, overturned carts and abandoned belongings is now a place of purposeful movement. Smoke rises from carefully managed cooking fires. Water barrels have been positioned beside the shelters, and the wounded have been moved into the driest buildings available. Children remain gathered beneath the granary awning, watched by older villagers who have volunteered to keep them occupied.

Most striking of all, the people who arrived at Highspire expecting to be protected have begun preparing to protect it themselves.

The lower wooden gates are reinforced with additional beams. Heavy carts have been turned sideways to create a second barricade, and gaps between the timber have been packed with broken stone and earth. The work is rough, but it has transformed the approach into a narrow passage that would be difficult for a large creature to force its way through.

You move along the barricade, checking the work and answering questions as they arise.

“That beam needs another brace,” you tell Tomas, pointing towards a section where the timber has begun to bow.

He wipes his forehead with the back of his hand.

“I know. I've been telling these two that for the last ten minutes.”

“Then perhaps they'll listen to me.”

The two villagers exchange glances before fetching another length of timber.

Tomas gives you a tired smile.

“You've become rather good at telling people what to do.”

“Someone has to.”

“Your father used to say the same thing.”

The mention of your family catches you unexpectedly. For a moment, the courtyard seems to recede, and you remember Highspire before the fires, before the ash, before the people around you had learned to recognise the sound of distant horns.

You force yourself to return to the work.

There will be time to remember later.

Inside the walls of Highspire Garrison, the atmosphere transforms dramatically. The once-panicked refugees are now a disciplined, armed auxiliary unit guarding the lower bailey.

With the armory fully unlocked and the quartermaster's reserves distributed, every volunteer holds cold-iron steel and stands ready behind newly reinforced timber barricades.

The weapons are not uniform. Some carry spears, others short swords or heavy shields. A few have been given bows, although the supply of arrows is limited. You have insisted that nobody be issued a weapon without basic instruction, and the more experienced villagers have spent the afternoon showing the others how to hold a shield, maintain a defensive line and avoid striking the person standing beside them.

The quartermaster initially objected to the distribution of military equipment. He changed his position after seeing the barricades and hearing how many people had volunteered to defend them.

“These are not soldiers,” he had protested.

“No,” you had replied. “They're people whose homes have already been destroyed. They have more reason than most to understand what happens if we fail.”

He had eventually handed over the reserve weapons, although not without making it clear that he intended to count every blade afterwards.

Through tense negotiation and sheer grit, you have forced the garrison commanders to acknowledge the refugees as equals in the upcoming defence.

The villagers have been given access to the tools and materials needed to strengthen the lower bailey, along with a limited number of weapons from the garrison stores. It is not enough to equip everyone, but you have organised the volunteers into groups with different responsibilities.

Those without weapons will carry water, move supplies and assist the wounded. Others will reinforce the barricades, maintain the fires and watch the approaches. The strongest volunteers have been assigned to the gates, where they can help the soldiers move heavy beams and prevent the barricades from being overturned.

Some of the garrison officers remain unhappy with the arrangement. You have heard their objections: civilians are unpredictable, frightened people make poor defenders, and the lower bailey is a military responsibility.

But none of them has offered a better solution.

The refugees have made it clear that they will not simply wait to be slaughtered if the walls fall. At least now they have a place in the defence, rather than being treated as an inconvenience behind it.

You climb onto the low stone platform beside the barricade and look over the courtyard.

The volunteers are beginning to understand the importance of working together. They have established simple signals for raising an alarm, agreed where the wounded should be taken and identified the safest route towards the inner keep if the lower gate is breached.

You notice Mara standing near the treatment shelter, speaking to a young soldier. Her sleeves are rolled up, and her hands are stained with herbs and blood. Elsie sits nearby beneath a blanket, helping to sort clean bandages into piles.

When Mara sees you, she gives a small nod.

It is not a smile. Neither of you has much reason to smile.

But there is recognition in it. You have helped create something that might keep her daughter alive.

A little further along, Tomas is testing the strength of the newly reinforced gate. He pushes against one of the beams with his shoulder, then gestures for two other villagers to join him.

The timber holds.

“That'll do,” he announces. “Unless they've brought a battering ram the size of the bloody keep.”

A few people laugh. The sound is brief, but it matters. For the first time since Highspire burned, the courtyard contains something other than fear.

Your companion approaches from the far end of the barricade, carrying a bundle of spare leather straps. Their expression is tired, and there is a fresh scrape across one knuckle.

“You've managed to turn half the village into soldiers,” they say.

“Auxiliary defenders.”

“That sounds considerably less impressive.”

“It is considerably more accurate.”

They glance towards the volunteers, then back at you.

“You've done well. They needed someone to give them something to do.”

You look down at the muddy ground. “They did the work themselves.”

“Perhaps. But they followed you.”

For a moment, neither of you speaks. The sounds of the courtyard continue around you: the clatter of tools, the scrape of timber and the low murmur of people preparing for a battle they cannot avoid.

Your companion reaches out and briefly touches your arm.

“Whatever happens tonight, you won't be standing here alone.”

The words are quiet, almost lost beneath the noise. You meet their gaze, aware of the weight behind the promise, before turning back towards the approaching soldiers.

A familiar figure passes you carrying a stack of folded blankets. They pause long enough to ask whether the treatment shelter needs anything else, then disappear into the crowd before you can answer properly.

You watch them go, aware that the people who matter to you are somewhere within these walls, depending on the same uncertain defences as everyone else.

You cannot protect them by worrying. You can only keep working.

A sharp command rings out from the upper wall.

“Make way!”

The volunteers step aside as a group of garrison soldiers enter the bailey carrying a heavy wooden chest. Behind them walks Commander Vane.

He has removed his helmet, revealing a face marked by fatigue and a thin cut above his left eyebrow. His armour is scratched, and there is dried mud along the hem of his coat. He looks first at the barricades, then at the organised groups of villagers and finally at you.

“Well,” he says. “This is rather different from the courtyard I left this morning.”

“The refugees needed somewhere to stand,” you reply.

Vane studies the lower gate.

“And you've given them somewhere to stand behind.”

He approaches the nearest barricade and tests one of the supports with his gloved hand. It does not move.

“Who organised this?”

“Tomas and the others built most of it. Mara organised the treatment shelter. The volunteers divided themselves into watches.”

“And you?”

You hesitate.

“I made sure they knew what needed doing.”

Vane gives a slow nod.

“That is often the hardest part.”

He turns towards the soldiers carrying the chest.

“Put those beside the gate. We have spare shield fittings and another supply of bolts. The volunteers will need them if they're expected to hold this position.”

One of the officers accompanying him looks uncomfortable.

“Commander, surely the civilians should be moved into the inner keep. We cannot risk them being caught in the fighting.”

Vane's expression hardens.

“And where, exactly, would you have them go? The inner keep is already filling with wounded and essential personnel. If the lower bailey falls, those people will be trapped regardless. Better that they know their positions and have a chance to defend themselves.”

The officer says nothing further.

Vane turns back to you.

“I have no intention of pretending these people are trained soldiers. But they have done more in a few hours than some of my own men have managed in a day. Keep them organised. Keep them away from the exposed wall-walk, and make sure every group knows where to fall back if the lower gate is breached.”

You nod.

“Understood.”

He studies you for another moment.

“There are reports from the northern watch. The fog is moving down from the mountains.”

The courtyard seems to quiet around you.

You look towards the narrow strip of sky visible above the walls. The light has begun to fade, and a grey haze is gathering beyond the distant rooftops. At first it resembles ordinary evening mist, but there is something wrong with the way it moves. It does not drift with the wind. It pours steadily down the slopes, filling the spaces between the trees and swallowing the road.

A horn sounds from the northern tower.

Then another answers from the western wall.

Vane puts his helmet back on.

“Positions.”

The order travels through the bailey. Soldiers move towards the stairs, and the volunteers begin taking their places behind the barricades. Tomas checks the gate supports one final time. Mara gathers the wounded deeper beneath the shelter. Your companion looks towards the fog, their expression suddenly serious.

You climb the steps towards the battlements.

Below you, the lower bailey is no longer a collection of frightened strangers. It is a community preparing to defend itself.

Above you, Highspire's soldiers take their places along the stone wall.

And beyond the valley, something is coming through the mist.

choices.text: Stand with Commander Vane on the battlements as the valley fog rolls in.
